<!-- theorema-1: body_md -->
Let $\mathfrak{L}$ be a Lie algebra over a field $\mathbb{F}$ of characteristic zero.
\begin{enumerate}
\item If $\mathfrak{L}$ is two-step nilpotent, in particular if $\mathfrak{L}$ is a Heisenberg algebra of arbitrary
dimension, then every linear map on $\mathfrak{L}$ is a $\mathrm{Hom}$-Lie structure.  (For Heisenberg algebras
this should be compared with the description of the \emph{multiplicative} $\mathrm{Hom}$-Lie structures
in \cite[Theorem 3.3]{Saa}; see Remark \ref{rem:heisknown}.)
\item If $\dim \mathfrak{L}=n<\infty$, then
$$\dim \mathcal{H}(\mathfrak{L}) \geq \max\Big\{\, n \cdot \dim \mathcal{C}(\mathfrak{L}), \ \
n^2-\binom{n}{3}\dim \mathfrak{L}^3 \,\Big\},$$
where $\mathfrak{L}^3=[\mathfrak{L},[\mathfrak{L},\mathfrak{L}]]$ and $\mathcal{C}(\mathfrak{L})$ is the centralizer of $[\mathfrak{L},\mathfrak{L}]$ in
$\mathfrak{L}$; the first bound holds because every linear map $\mathfrak{L} \to \mathcal{C}(\mathfrak{L})$ is a
$\mathrm{Hom}$-Lie structure.  In particular, if $\dim \mathfrak{L}=3$, then the $\mathrm{Hom}$-Lie structures of $\mathfrak{L}$
form a subspace of $\mathrm{End}(\mathfrak{L})$ of dimension at least $6$.
\item The bound in $(2)$ is attained for $n=3$ on $\mathfrak{sl}_2=\langle h,e,f\rangle$: writing
$\varphi(h)=a_1h+a_2e+a_3f$, $\varphi(e)=b_1h+b_2e+b_3f$ and $\varphi(f)=c_1h+c_2e+c_3f$, the map
$\varphi$ is a $\mathrm{Hom}$-Lie structure if and only if $b_2=c_3$, $a_2=2c_1$ and $a_3=2b_1$.  Part
$(3)$ is not new: it is \cite[Theorem 3.3]{xjl15} (see also \cite[Theorem 3.1]{xl17}), which we
recover here by a direct computation; see Remark \ref{rem:sl2known}.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end theorema-1 -->
<!-- theoremb-1: body_md -->
Let $\mathfrak{L}_{\lambda}$ be the $(2n+2)$-dimensional oscillator Lie algebra.  Then the $\mathrm{Hom}$-Lie
structures of $\mathfrak{L}_{\lambda}$ are precisely the maps listed in Theorem \ref{thm:osc}.
Let $\mathfrak{L}$ be a solvable Lie algebra with abelian nilpotent radical $\mathfrak{N}$ of codimension $1$ and
$\dim \mathfrak{N} \geq 2$.  Then a linear map on $\mathfrak{L}$ is a $\mathrm{Hom}$-Lie structure if and only if it
preserves $\mathfrak{N}$.
<!-- end theoremb-1 -->
<!-- theoremc-1: body_md -->
Let $\mathfrak{W}$ be the Witt algebra and $\mathfrak{V}$ its universal central extension, the Virasoro algebra.
\begin{enumerate}
\item A linear map $\varphi$ on $\mathfrak{W}$ is a $\mathrm{Hom}$-Lie structure if and only if
$\varphi(e_i)=\sum_{j \in \mathbb{Z}}\alpha_j e_{i+j}$ for all $i \in \mathbb{Z}$, where only finitely many
coefficients $\alpha_j$ are non-zero and they do not depend on $i$.  Part $(1)$ is not new: it
is \cite[Theorem 3.2]{xl17}, recovered here by a direct computation; see Remark
\ref{rem:wittknown}.
\item A linear map $\varphi$ on $\mathfrak{V}$ is a $\mathrm{Hom}$-Lie structure if and only if
$\varphi(x)=\alpha x+f(x)c$ for some scalar $\alpha$ and some linear form $f$ on $\mathfrak{V}$, i.e. if
and only if $\varphi$ is scalar modulo the centre.  Consequently, every transposed Poisson
structure on $\mathfrak{V}$ is trivial.  Part $(2)$ is the exact analogue, for the Virasoro algebra, of
the description of the $\mathrm{Hom}$-Lie structures of an affine Kac--Moody algebra given in
\cite[Theorem 3]{MZ18}; the Virasoro algebra is not an affine Kac--Moody algebra and is not
covered by loc. cit., and the result is obtained here independently (see Remark
\ref{rem:virkm}).  The last assertion is \cite[Corollary 28]{FKL21}, recovered here from the
description of
$\mathcal{H}(\mathfrak{V})$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end theoremc-1 -->
<!-- theoremd-1: body_md -->
Every $\frac12$-derivation of a Lie algebra $\mathfrak{L}$ is a $\mathrm{Hom}$-Lie structure, i.e.
$\Delta(\mathfrak{L})\subseteq \mathcal{H}(\mathfrak{L})$; more generally, for $\delta\neq0,1$ every
$\delta$-derivation of a Lie algebra is a $\mathrm{Hom}$-Lie structure (Filippov \cite{Fil98}).
The inclusion may be strict, and the quotient may be
arbitrarily large.  More generally, let $\delta \neq 0,1$ and let $A$ be an algebra of a variety
defined by multilinear identities of degree at most three.  Then every $\delta$-derivation of $A$
is a $\mathrm{Hom}$-structure of the corresponding $\mathrm{Hom}$-variety; in particular, $\delta$-derivations of
Lie, associative, left-symmetric, Novikov, Leibniz, Zinbiel, bicommutative and
$\delta'$-Novikov algebras (the Lie case being Filippov's theorem) are $\mathrm{Hom}$-Lie, $\mathrm{Hom}$-associative, $\mathrm{Hom}$-left-symmetric,
$\mathrm{Hom}$-Novikov, $\mathrm{Hom}$-Leibniz, $\mathrm{Hom}$-Zinbiel, $\mathrm{Hom}$-bicommutative and $\mathrm{Hom}$-$\delta'$-Novikov
structures respectively.
<!-- end theoremd-1 -->
<!-- theoreme-1: body_md -->
Let $\Gamma$ be a non-trivial additive subgroup of $\mathbb{F}$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item A graded shift of degree $t$ of the algebra $W(\Gamma;a,b)$, i.e. a map
$L_{\mu}\mapsto \alpha L_{\mu+t}+\beta I_{\mu+t}$, $I_{\mu}\mapsto \gamma I_{\mu+t}$, is a
$\mathrm{Hom}$-Lie structure if and only if $\gamma=\alpha$ and $\alpha t(b^2-1)=0$.
\item A graded shift of degree $t$ of the deformative Schr\"odinger--Witt algebra
$\mathcal{S}(\Gamma;a,b)$, i.e. a map $L_{\mu}\mapsto \alpha L_{\mu+t}+\beta I_{\mu+t}$,
$I_{\mu}\mapsto \gamma I_{\mu+t}$, $Y_{\mu}\mapsto \delta Y_{\mu+t}$, is a $\mathrm{Hom}$-Lie structure
if and only if $\gamma=\delta=\alpha$ and $\alpha t(b+1)=0$.
\item Every map $L_{\mu}\mapsto \beta I_{\mu+t}$, $I_{\mu},Y_{\mu}\mapsto 0$ is a $\mathrm{Hom}$-Lie
structure of the algebras in $(1)$ and $(2)$, for all values of $a$ and $b$; likewise every map
$L_m \mapsto \beta M_{m+t}$, $M_n,N_n,Y_{n+\frac12}\mapsto 0$ is a $\mathrm{Hom}$-Lie structure of the
extended Schr\"odinger--Witt algebra, which has no non-trivial $\frac12$-derivation.
\item Every translation invariant map
$L_{\alpha,i}\mapsto \sum_{d,m}c_{d,m}L_{\alpha+d,i+m}$ is a $\mathrm{Hom}$-Lie structure of the
not-finitely graded Witt algebra $W_n(G)$.  On the Heisenberg--Witt algebra $HW_n(G)$ with
$n \neq 0$, by contrast, a graded shift acting by the same non-zero scalar on the $L$'s and on
the $H$'s is a $\mathrm{Hom}$-Lie structure only if the shift is trivial, while all the maps
$L_{\alpha,i}\mapsto \beta H_{\alpha+d,i+m}$, $H_{\alpha,i}\mapsto 0$ are $\mathrm{Hom}$-Lie structures.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end theoreme-1 -->
<!-- theoremf-1: body_md -->
Let $\widehat{\mathfrak{L}}=\mathfrak{L} \oplus Z$ be a central extension of a Lie algebra $\mathfrak{L}$ by a $2$-cocycle
$\omega$.  A linear map $\varphi$ of $\widehat{\mathfrak{L}}$ with $\varphi(Z)\subseteq Z$ is a $\mathrm{Hom}$-Lie
structure if and only if its $\mathfrak{L}$-part $\psi$ is a $\mathrm{Hom}$-Lie structure of $\mathfrak{L}$ and
$\sum_{\mathrm{cyc}}\omega(\psi(x),[y,z])=0$.  Evaluating this obstruction on graded shifts one
obtains, for the central extensions listed above:
\begin{enumerate}
\item for $g(G,\lambda)$: the shift $L_a \mapsto \alpha L_{a+t}+\beta I_{a+t}$,
$I_a \mapsto \gamma I_{a+t}$ is a $\mathrm{Hom}$-Lie structure if and only if $\gamma=\alpha$ and
$\alpha t=0$, and moreover $\beta t=0$ for $\lambda=1$ and $\beta=0$ for $\lambda=0$ and for
$\lambda=-2$ of rank $\geq 2$; in particular, on the twisted Heisenberg--Virasoro algebra all
graded shifts which are $\mathrm{Hom}$-Lie structures are scalar modulo the centre;
\item for $\widehat{W}(G)$: the shift $L_{\alpha,i}\mapsto cL_{\alpha+d,i+m}$ is a $\mathrm{Hom}$-Lie
structure if and only if $m \geq 1$ or $cd=0$, which reproduces exactly the description of
$\Delta(\widehat{W}(G))$ of \cite{KKhS24b};
\item for $\widetilde{W}(G)$: only the shifts with $cd=cm=0$, i.e. the maps which are scalar
modulo the centre;
\item for the extended Schr\"odinger--Virasoro algebra $\hat{\mathfrak{so}}$ and for the
algebras $\widetilde{L_{\lambda,\mu}}^{\,i}$, $i \in \{1,2,3,5\}$: the maps
$L_m \mapsto \beta M_{m+t}$ survive for every $t$, so that these algebras carry
infinite-dimensional spaces of $\mathrm{Hom}$-Lie structures modulo the centre --- although all of them,
with the single exception of $\widetilde{L_{1,\mu}}^{\,1}$, have no non-trivial
$\frac12$-derivation at all; for $\widetilde{L_{1,\mu}}^{\,4}$ only the single value $t=-2\mu$
survives.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end theoremf-1 -->
<!-- theoremg-1: body_md -->
The following algebras, whose $\frac12$-derivations and transposed Poisson structures have
recently been described in the literature, have the following spaces of $\mathrm{Hom}$-Lie structures.
\begin{enumerate}
\item (Dimension three.)  For every three-dimensional Lie algebra $\mathfrak{L}$ the space
$\mathcal{H}(\mathfrak{L})$ has codimension exactly $\dim \mathfrak{L}^3$ in $\mathrm{End}(\mathfrak{L})$, i.e.
$\dim \mathcal{H}(\mathfrak{L})=9-\dim \mathfrak{L}^3$; over an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero
the possible values are $9$ (two-step nilpotent algebras), $8$, $7$ and $6$ (only $\mathfrak{sl}_2$).
Compare with the classification of the three-dimensional transposed Poisson algebras
\cite{BFOK}.
\item (Matrices.)  For the Lie algebra $M_n(\mathbb{F})$ of all $n \times n$ matrices over an
algebraically closed field of characteristic zero,
$\mathcal{H}(M_n(\mathbb{F}))=\mathbb{F}\,\mathrm{id} \oplus \mathrm{Hom}(M_n(\mathbb{F}),Z)$ for $n \geq 3$, of dimension $n^2+1$,
and $\dim \mathcal{H}(M_2(\mathbb{F}))=10$.  For the Lie algebra $T_n(\mathbb{F})$ of upper triangular matrices
and $n \geq 4$,
$$\mathcal{H}(T_n(\mathbb{F}))=\mathrm{Hom}\big(T_n(\mathbb{F}),\langle \delta,e_{1n}\rangle\big)\oplus
\langle \mathrm{id},A,B,A',B'\rangle, \qquad \dim \mathcal{H}(T_n(\mathbb{F}))=n(n+1)+5,$$
where $A,B,A',B'$ are the four explicit maps of Definition \ref{def:tnmaps}.  In both cases the
space of $\frac12$-derivations, computed in \cite{KKhUT}, is much smaller: of dimension $2$,
resp. $n+2$.
\item (Virasoro-like algebras.)  The Virasoro-like algebra $\mathcal{V}$, with basis
$\{L_m\}_{m \in \mathbb{Z}^2\setminus\{0\}}$ and $[L_m,L_n]=(m_1n_2-m_2n_1)L_{m+n}$, and its
$q$-analogue $\mathcal{V}_q$ with $q$ not a root of unity, admit only trivial $\mathrm{Hom}$-Lie
structures:
$\mathcal{H}(\mathcal{V})=\mathcal{H}(\mathcal{V}_q)=\mathbb{F}\,\mathrm{id}$.  Consequently they admit no
non-trivial transposed Poisson structure, which recovers results of \cite{LLJ1,LLJ2}.  This is
the opposite behaviour to that of the Witt algebra, for which
$\Delta(\mathfrak{W})=\mathcal{H}(\mathfrak{W})$ is infinite-dimensional.
\item (Planar Galilean conformal algebra.)  A graded shift of degree $t$ of
$\mathcal{G}(\Gamma)$ is a $\mathrm{Hom}$-Lie structure if and only if it is of the form
$L_{\mu}\mapsto \alpha L_{\mu+t}+\beta I_{\mu+t}+\gamma J_{\mu+t}$,
$H_{\mu}\mapsto \alpha H_{\mu+t}$, $I_{\mu}\mapsto \alpha I_{\mu+t}$,
$J_{\mu}\mapsto \alpha J_{\mu+t}$ with $\alpha t=0$.  In particular
$\mathcal{H}(\mathcal{G}(\Gamma))$ is infinite-dimensional, although all the
$\frac12$-derivations and all the transposed Poisson structures of $\mathcal{G}(\mathbb{Z})$ are
trivial \cite{WZ}.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end theoremg-1 -->
<!-- definition-1: body_md -->
\label{def:hom}
Let $(\mathfrak{L},[\cdot,\cdot])$ be a Lie algebra and let $\varphi \colon \mathfrak{L} \to \mathfrak{L}$ be a linear map.
Then $(\mathfrak{L},[\cdot,\cdot],\varphi)$ is a \emph{$\mathrm{Hom}$-Lie structure} on $(\mathfrak{L},[\cdot,\cdot])$ if
\begin{equation}\label{HOM}
[\varphi(x),[y,z]]+[\varphi(y),[z,x]]+[\varphi(z),[x,y]]=0
\qquad \text{for all } x,y,z \in \mathfrak{L} .
\end{equation}
A $\mathrm{Hom}$-Lie structure is \emph{trivial} if $\varphi$ is a scalar multiple of the identity map.
<!-- end definition-1 -->
<!-- lemma-1: body_md -->
\label{lem:alt}
For every $\varphi \in \mathrm{End}(\mathfrak{L})$ the map $E_{\varphi}$ is trilinear and alternating: it is
invariant under cyclic permutations of $(x,y,z)$, it changes sign under each transposition of two
of its arguments, and it vanishes whenever two of its arguments are equal.
<!-- end lemma-1 -->
<!-- corollary-1: body_md -->
\label{cor:triples}
Let $\{e_i\}_{i \in I}$ be a basis of $\mathfrak{L}$ indexed by a linearly ordered set $I$.  A linear map
$\varphi \in \mathrm{End}(\mathfrak{L})$ is a $\mathrm{Hom}$-Lie structure on $\mathfrak{L}$ if and only if
$E_{\varphi}(e_i,e_j,e_k)=0$ for all $i<j<k$.
<!-- end corollary-1 -->
<!-- lemma-2: body_md -->
\label{lem:subspace}
The $\mathrm{Hom}$-Lie structures on a Lie algebra $\mathfrak{L}$ form a linear subspace $\mathcal{H}(\mathfrak{L})$ of
$\mathrm{End}(\mathfrak{L})$.  It contains all scalar maps $\alpha\,\mathrm{id}$ and all linear maps whose image lies in
the centre of $\mathfrak{L}$.
<!-- end lemma-2 -->
<!-- lemma-3: body_md -->
\label{lem:mult}
Let $\cdot$ be a transposed Poisson structure on a Lie algebra $(\mathfrak{L},[\cdot,\cdot])$.  Then
$\mathcal{M}_a$ is a $\mathrm{Hom}$-Lie structure on $(\mathfrak{L},[\cdot,\cdot])$ for every $a \in \mathfrak{L}$.
<!-- end lemma-3 -->
<!-- proposition-1: body_md -->
\label{prop:homtr}
Let $(\mathfrak{L},[\cdot,\cdot])$ be a Lie algebra with $\dim \mathfrak{L} \geq 2$, i.e. $\mathfrak{L}$ is not spanned by a
single element.  If $\mathfrak{L}$ admits no non-trivial $\mathrm{Hom}$-Lie structure, then $\mathfrak{L}$ admits no
non-trivial transposed Poisson structure.
<!-- end proposition-1 -->
<!-- remark-1: body_md -->
\label{rem:homtr}
The hypothesis $\dim \mathfrak{L} \geq 2$ cannot be omitted.  On a one-dimensional (abelian) Lie algebra
$\mathfrak{L} = \langle e \rangle$ every linear map is a scalar multiple of the identity, so all
$\mathrm{Hom}$-Lie structures are trivial, while the field multiplication $e \cdot e = e$ is a
non-trivial transposed Poisson structure.
<!-- end remark-1 -->
<!-- definition-2: body_md -->
\label{def:half}
A linear map $\varphi \in \mathrm{End}(\mathfrak{L})$ is a \emph{$\frac12$-derivation} of the Lie algebra $\mathfrak{L}$ if
$$\varphi([x,y])=\tfrac12\big([\varphi(x),y]+[x,\varphi(y)]\big) \qquad \text{for all }
x,y \in \mathfrak{L} .$$
The space of $\frac12$-derivations of $\mathfrak{L}$ is denoted by $\Delta(\mathfrak{L})$.
<!-- end definition-2 -->
<!-- theorem-1: body_md -->
\label{thm:half}
Every $\frac12$-derivation of a Lie algebra is a $\mathrm{Hom}$-Lie structure; that is,
$$\Delta(\mathfrak{L}) \subseteq \mathcal{H}(\mathfrak{L})$$
for every Lie algebra $\mathfrak{L}$.
<!-- end theorem-1 -->
<!-- remark-2: body_md -->
\label{rem:halfstrict}
The inclusion of Theorem \ref{thm:half} is in general strict, and very far from being an
equality.  For $\mathfrak{sl}_2$ one has $\Delta(\mathfrak{sl}_2)=\langle \mathrm{id} \rangle$, whereas
$\mathcal{H}(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ is $6$-dimensional by Theorem \ref{thm:sl2}.  Sections
\ref{sec:wab}--\ref{sec:nfg} below exhibit whole families of algebras with
$\Delta(\mathfrak{L})=\langle \mathrm{id} \rangle$ and $\mathcal{H}(\mathfrak{L})$ infinite-dimensional.
<!-- end remark-2 -->
<!-- definition-3: body_md -->
\label{def:delta}
Let $\delta \in \mathbb{F}$.  A linear map $\varphi \in \mathrm{End}(A)$ is a \emph{$\delta$-derivation} of $A$
if
$$\varphi(xy)=\delta\big(\varphi(x)y+x\varphi(y)\big) \qquad \text{for all } x,y \in A .$$
<!-- end definition-3 -->
<!-- definition-4: body_md -->
\label{def:homvar}
A \emph{multilinear polynomial of degree three} is an expression
$$f(x_1,x_2,x_3)=\sum_{\sigma \in S_3}\Big(a_{\sigma}\,(x_{\sigma(1)}x_{\sigma(2)})x_{\sigma(3)}
+b_{\sigma}\,x_{\sigma(1)}(x_{\sigma(2)}x_{\sigma(3)})\Big), \qquad a_{\sigma},b_{\sigma}\in \mathbb{F} .$$
For $\varphi \in \mathrm{End}(A)$ its \emph{$\mathrm{Hom}$-version} is obtained by applying $\varphi$ to the
outer variable of each monomial:
$$f^{\varphi}(x_1,x_2,x_3)=\sum_{\sigma \in S_3}\Big(a_{\sigma}\,(x_{\sigma(1)}x_{\sigma(2)})
\varphi(x_{\sigma(3)})+b_{\sigma}\,\varphi(x_{\sigma(1)})(x_{\sigma(2)}x_{\sigma(3)})\Big).$$
Let $\mathcal{V}$ be a variety of algebras defined by a family of multilinear identities of
degrees two and three.  A linear map $\varphi$ on an algebra $A \in \mathcal{V}$ is a
\emph{$\mathrm{Hom}$-$\mathcal{V}$ structure} on $A$ if $f^{\varphi}(x,y,z)=0$ for all $x,y,z\in A$ and
every defining identity $f$ of degree three (the identities of degree two, such as commutativity
or anticommutativity, are not twisted).
<!-- end definition-4 -->
<!-- lemma-4: body_md -->
\label{lem:deltamon}
Let $\varphi$ be a $\delta$-derivation of $A$.  Then for all $a,b,c \in A$
$$\varphi\big((ab)c\big)=\delta^{2}\big((\varphi(a)b)c+(a\varphi(b))c+(ab)\varphi(c)\big)
+\delta(1-\delta)\,(ab)\varphi(c),$$
$$\varphi\big(a(bc)\big)=\delta^{2}\big(\varphi(a)(bc)+a(\varphi(b)c)+a(b\varphi(c))\big)
+\delta(1-\delta)\,\varphi(a)(bc).$$
Consequently, for every multilinear polynomial $f$ of degree three,
$$\varphi\big(f(x,y,z)\big)=\delta^{2}\big(f(\varphi(x),y,z)+f(x,\varphi(y),z)+f(x,y,\varphi(z))\big)
+\delta(1-\delta)\,f^{\varphi}(x,y,z).$$
<!-- end lemma-4 -->
<!-- theorem-2: body_md -->
\label{thm:delta}
Let $\delta \in \mathbb{F}\setminus\{0,1\}$ and let $f$ be a multilinear identity of degree three of the
algebra $A$.  Then every $\delta$-derivation $\varphi$ of $A$ satisfies
$f^{\varphi}(x,y,z)=0$ for all $x,y,z\in A$.  In particular, if $A$ belongs to a variety
$\mathcal{V}$ defined by multilinear identities of degrees two and three, then every
$\delta$-derivation of $A$ is a $\mathrm{Hom}$-$\mathcal{V}$ structure on $A$.
<!-- end theorem-2 -->
<!-- corollary-2: body_md -->
\label{cor:deltavar}
Let $\delta \neq 0,1$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item \textup{(Filippov \cite{Fil98})} Every $\delta$-derivation of a Lie algebra $\mathfrak{L}$ is a
$\mathrm{Hom}$-Lie structure on $\mathfrak{L}$.  For $\delta=\frac12$ this is Theorem \ref{thm:half}.
\item Every $\delta$-derivation of an associative algebra is a $\mathrm{Hom}$-associative structure in the
sense of \cite{MS08}.
\item Every $\delta$-derivation of a left-symmetric (respectively Novikov) algebra is a
$\mathrm{Hom}$-left-symmetric (respectively $\mathrm{Hom}$-Novikov) structure in the sense of \cite{Yau11}.
\item Every $\delta$-derivation of a Leibniz, Zinbiel or bicommutative algebra, and of a
$\delta'$-Novikov algebra in the sense of \cite{Kay25,AKL25} for any $\delta'$, is a
$\mathrm{Hom}$-structure of the corresponding variety, in the sense of Definition \ref{def:homvar}.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end corollary-2 -->
<!-- remark-3: body_md -->
\label{rem:deltaexc}
The hypothesis $\delta\neq 0,1$ cannot be dropped.  For $\delta=1$: the derivation
$\varphi=\mathrm{ad}_e$ of $\mathfrak{sl}_2$ is given by $\varphi(h)=-2e$, $\varphi(e)=0$, $\varphi(f)=h$;
in the notation of Theorem \ref{thm:sl2} it has $a_2=-2$ and $c_1=1$, so $a_2\neq 2c_1$ and
$\varphi$ is not a $\mathrm{Hom}$-Lie structure.  For $\delta=0$ the $0$-derivations are just the linear
maps vanishing on $A^2$, and Lemma \ref{lem:deltamon} gives no information.  Theorem
\ref{thm:delta} also says nothing about identities of degree four or higher, such as the Jordan or
the Mal'tsev identity.  Finally, Theorem \ref{thm:delta} extends verbatim to even
$\delta$-superderivations of superalgebras and the super-versions of the identities, since an
even map does not change the parities of the arguments; thus the even $\delta$-superderivations
($\delta\neq0,1$) computed, for instance, in \cite{Kay09,Kay10,Zus10,YT24a,HGS25} provide
$\mathrm{Hom}$-structures on the corresponding Lie superalgebras.
<!-- end remark-3 -->
<!-- remark-4: body_md -->
\label{rem:deltalit}
By Corollary \ref{cor:deltavar}, every known description of the $\delta$-derivations of a Lie
algebra with $\delta\neq 0,1$ --- for example those of \cite{Fil98,Fil99,Zus10,WC26,CY25,LLJ2}
--- yields $\mathrm{Hom}$-Lie structures, and $\delta$-derivations ($\delta\neq0,1$) of commutative
associative algebras,
which are the main tool of the constructions of \cite{Kay25,AKS26}, are
$\mathrm{Hom}$-associative structures.
<!-- end remark-4 -->
<!-- corollary-3: body_md -->
\label{cor:dim2}
If $\dim \mathfrak{L} \leq 2$, then every linear map $\varphi \colon \mathfrak{L} \to \mathfrak{L}$ is a $\mathrm{Hom}$-Lie
structure, i.e. $\mathcal{H}(\mathfrak{L})=\mathrm{End}(\mathfrak{L})$.
<!-- end corollary-3 -->
<!-- proposition-2: body_md -->
\label{prop:2step}
Let $\mathfrak{L}$ be two-step nilpotent, i.e. $[\mathfrak{L},[\mathfrak{L},\mathfrak{L}]]=0$.  Then every linear map
$\varphi \colon \mathfrak{L} \to \mathfrak{L}$ is a $\mathrm{Hom}$-Lie structure.  In particular this holds for every
abelian Lie algebra and for every Heisenberg algebra
$$\mathfrak{H}(V,\omega)=V \oplus \langle z \rangle, \qquad [v,w]=\omega(v,w)z, \qquad [v,z]=0
\qquad (v,w \in V),$$
associated with a skew-symmetric bilinear form $\omega$ on a vector space $V$ of arbitrary,
possibly infinite, dimension.
<!-- end proposition-2 -->
<!-- remark-5: body_md -->
\label{rem:heisknown}
For Heisenberg algebras Proposition \ref{prop:2step} should be compared with
\cite[Theorem 3.3]{Saa}, where the $\mathrm{Hom}$-Lie algebras whose underlying Lie algebra is the
$(2m+1)$-dimensional Heisenberg algebra $\mathfrak{H}_m=\langle x_1,\dots,x_m,y_1,\dots,y_m,z\rangle$,
$[x_k,y_k]=z$, are determined.  There the twisting map $\alpha$ is required to be
\emph{multiplicative}, i.e. to be in addition an endomorphism of $\mathfrak{H}_m$, and the answer is that
the matrix of $\alpha$ in the above basis has the block shape
$$P=\begin{pmatrix} X & T & 0 \\ Z & Y & 0 \\ L & M & \lambda \end{pmatrix},
\qquad \begin{pmatrix} X & T \\ Z & Y \end{pmatrix} \ \ \lambda\text{-symplectic} ,$$
that is, $\alpha(z)=\lambda z$ and the map induced by $\alpha$ on $V=\langle x_1,\dots,y_m\rangle$
multiplies the symplectic form by $\lambda$.  The two statements are consistent and
complementary.  Indeed, by Proposition \ref{prop:2step} the $\mathrm{Hom}$-Jacobi identity (\ref{HOM})
imposes no condition at all on a linear map of a two-step nilpotent algebra, so that in the
Heisenberg case the entire content of \cite[Theorem 3.3]{Saa} is the multiplicativity
requirement $\alpha([u,v])=[\alpha(u),\alpha(v)]$: for $u,v \in V$ this reads
$\omega(u,v)\alpha(z)=\omega(\alpha(u),\alpha(v))z$, which is precisely the condition that
$\alpha(z)=\lambda z$ and that the $V$-block be $\lambda$-symplectic.  Without the
multiplicativity assumption --- which is the setting of Definition \ref{def:hom} and of the
present paper --- the $\mathrm{Hom}$-Lie structures of $\mathfrak{H}_m$ form the whole space $\mathrm{End}(\mathfrak{H}_m)$, of
dimension $(2m+1)^2$; and Proposition \ref{prop:2step} covers in addition the Heisenberg
algebras $\mathfrak{H}(V,\omega)$ of infinite dimension and all two-step nilpotent algebras.
<!-- end remark-5 -->
<!-- remark-6: body_md -->
\label{rem:heis}
Heisenberg algebras also carry many non-trivial transposed Poisson structures.  Let $f$ be a
non-zero linear form on $V$ and put
$$(v+az)\cdot(w+bz)=f(v)f(w)\,z, \qquad v,w \in V, \ a,b \in \mathbb{F} .$$
This multiplication is commutative, and it is associative because both
$((v+az)\cdot(w+bz))\cdot(u+cz)$ and $(v+az)\cdot((w+bz)\cdot(u+cz))$ are multiples of $f(z)=0$.
The transposed Leibniz rule (\ref{TP}) holds as well: its left-hand side vanishes because
$[x,y] \in \langle z \rangle$ and $f(z)=0$, and its right-hand side vanishes because the products
$z'\cdot x$ and $z'\cdot y$ are central.  This is consistent with Proposition \ref{prop:homtr}:
by Proposition \ref{prop:2step} the algebra $\mathfrak{H}(V,\omega)$ has plenty of non-trivial $\mathrm{Hom}$-Lie
structures.
<!-- end remark-6 -->
<!-- proposition-3: body_md -->
\label{prop:centralizer}
Let $\mathfrak{L}$ be an arbitrary Lie algebra.  Then every linear map
$\varphi \colon \mathfrak{L} \to \mathcal{C}(\mathfrak{L})$ is a $\mathrm{Hom}$-Lie structure, i.e.
$$\mathrm{Hom}(\mathfrak{L},\mathcal{C}(\mathfrak{L})) \subseteq \mathcal{H}(\mathfrak{L}).$$
If $\dim \mathfrak{L} = n < \infty$, then consequently
$$\dim \mathcal{H}(\mathfrak{L}) \geq n \cdot \dim \mathcal{C}(\mathfrak{L}).$$
<!-- end proposition-3 -->
<!-- theorem-3: body_md -->
\label{thm:dimn}
Let $\mathfrak{L}$ be a Lie algebra of dimension $n$ with basis $\{e_1,\ldots,e_n\}$.  For
$1 \leq i<j<k \leq n$ put
$$V_{ijk}=\big[\mathfrak{L},\ \langle [e_i,e_j],\,[e_j,e_k],\,[e_k,e_i] \rangle\big] \subseteq \mathfrak{L}^3 .$$
Then the $\mathrm{Hom}$-Lie structures of $\mathfrak{L}$ form the kernel of the linear map
$$\Phi \colon \mathrm{End}(\mathfrak{L}) \longrightarrow \bigoplus_{1 \leq i<j<k \leq n} V_{ijk}, \qquad
\Phi(\varphi)=\big(E_{\varphi}(e_i,e_j,e_k)\big)_{1 \leq i<j<k \leq n},$$
and therefore
$$\dim \mathcal{H}(\mathfrak{L}) \ \geq \ n^2-\sum_{1 \leq i<j<k \leq n} \dim V_{ijk}
\ \geq \ n^2-\binom{n}{3}\dim \mathfrak{L}^3 .$$
<!-- end theorem-3 -->
<!-- corollary-4: body_md -->
\label{cor:dimn}
For every Lie algebra $\mathfrak{L}$ of finite dimension $n$,
$$\dim \mathcal{H}(\mathfrak{L}) \ \geq \
\max\Big\{\, n \cdot \dim \mathcal{C}(\mathfrak{L}),\ \ n^2-\binom{n}{3}\dim \mathfrak{L}^3 \,\Big\}.$$
In particular:
\begin{enumerate}
\item if $n \leq 2$, then $\binom{n}{3}=0$ and $\mathcal{H}(\mathfrak{L})=\mathrm{End}(\mathfrak{L})$ (Corollary
\ref{cor:dim2});
\item if $\mathfrak{L}$ is two-step nilpotent, then $\mathfrak{L}^3=0$ and $\mathcal{H}(\mathfrak{L})=\mathrm{End}(\mathfrak{L})$
(Proposition \ref{prop:2step});
\item if $n=3$, then $\dim \mathfrak{L}^3 \leq 3$ and $\binom{3}{3}=1$, so
$\dim \mathcal{H}(\mathfrak{L})\geq 9-3=6$ (Theorem \ref{thm:dim3} below).
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end corollary-4 -->
<!-- remark-7: body_md -->
\label{rem:dimn}
The two bounds of Corollary \ref{cor:dimn} are of a complementary nature, and each of them is
vacuous in the range in which the other one is informative.

The bound $n^2-\binom{n}{3}\dim \mathfrak{L}^3$ is positive only for algebras which are close to being
two-step nilpotent: if $\dim \mathfrak{L}^3=d \geq 1$, it says something only when
$\binom{n}{3}d<n^2$, i.e. for $n \leq 8$ when $d=1$, for $n \leq 6$ when $d=2$, and for
$n \leq 5$ when $d=3$.  Its refined form $n^2-\sum_{i<j<k}\dim V_{ijk}$, however, keeps its
content in every dimension, because the triples $(i,j,k)$ with
$[e_i,e_j]=[e_j,e_k]=[e_k,e_i]=0$ --- which are the vast majority for a sparse multiplication
table --- contribute nothing at all; Example \ref{ex:fil4} shows that the refined bound can be
attained.

The bound $n \cdot \dim \mathcal{C}(\mathfrak{L})$, on the other hand, is informative exactly when the
derived subalgebra has a large centralizer; it gives nothing for algebras with
$\mathcal{C}(\mathfrak{L})=0$, such as $\mathfrak{sl}_2$ and, more generally, any semi-simple Lie algebra.
Example \ref{ex:sl2ab} exhibits, in every dimension $n \geq 3$, an algebra for which the first
bound misses the true value by exactly $6$ while the second one is vacuous as soon as
$n \geq 6$.
<!-- end remark-7 -->
<!-- example-1: body_md -->
\label{ex:fil4}
Let $\mathfrak{N}_4=\langle e_1,e_2,e_3,e_4\rangle$ be the four-dimensional filiform Lie algebra, with
multiplication
$$[e_1,e_2]=e_3, \qquad [e_1,e_3]=e_4$$
and all the remaining brackets of basis vectors equal to zero.  Then
$$\mathcal{H}(\mathfrak{N}_4)=\{\varphi \in \mathrm{End}(\mathfrak{N}_4) \ : \ \varphi(e_3),\varphi(e_4) \in
\langle e_2,e_3,e_4\rangle\}, \qquad \dim \mathcal{H}(\mathfrak{N}_4)=14,$$
and this is exactly the value given by the refined bound of Theorem \ref{thm:dimn}.
<!-- end example-1 -->
<!-- example-2: body_md -->
\label{ex:sl2ab}
Let $n \geq 3$, let $m=n-3$ and let $\mathfrak{L}_n=\mathfrak{sl}_2 \oplus A_m$ be the direct sum of $\mathfrak{sl}_2$ and
of an abelian Lie algebra $A_m=\langle a_1,\ldots,a_m\rangle$ of dimension $m$.  Then
$$\dim \mathcal{H}(\mathfrak{L}_n)=m^2+3m+6=n^2-3n+6=n \cdot \dim \mathcal{C}(\mathfrak{L}_n)+6 .$$
<!-- end example-2 -->
<!-- theorem-4: body_md -->
\label{thm:dim3}
Let $\mathfrak{L}$ be a three-dimensional Lie algebra with basis $\{e_1,e_2,e_3\}$.  Then the $\mathrm{Hom}$-Lie
structures of $\mathfrak{L}$ form the kernel of the linear map
$$\Phi \colon \mathrm{End}(\mathfrak{L}) \to \mathfrak{L}, \qquad \Phi(\varphi)=E_{\varphi}(e_1,e_2,e_3),$$
and therefore a subspace of $\mathrm{End}(\mathfrak{L})$ of dimension at least $9-3=6$.
<!-- end theorem-4 -->
<!-- theorem-5: body_md -->
\label{thm:sl2}
Write a linear map $\varphi$ on $\mathfrak{sl}_2$ as
$$\varphi(h)=a_1h+a_2e+a_3f, \qquad \varphi(e)=b_1h+b_2e+b_3f, \qquad
\varphi(f)=c_1h+c_2e+c_3f .$$
Then $\varphi$ is a $\mathrm{Hom}$-Lie structure if and only if
$$b_2=c_3, \qquad a_2=2c_1, \qquad a_3=2b_1 .$$
Consequently the $\mathrm{Hom}$-Lie structures of $\mathfrak{sl}_2$ form a $6$-dimensional space, parametrized
bijectively by $(a_1,b_1,b_2,b_3,c_1,c_2) \in \mathbb{F}^6$ through
$$\varphi(h)=a_1h+2c_1e+2b_1f, \qquad \varphi(e)=b_1h+b_2e+b_3f, \qquad
\varphi(f)=c_1h+c_2e+b_2f .$$
<!-- end theorem-5 -->
<!-- remark-8: body_md -->
\label{rem:sl2known}
Theorem \ref{thm:sl2} is not a new result: the space $\mathcal{H}(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ was computed by Xie,
Jin and Liu \cite[Theorem 3.3]{xjl15}, and their answer is reproduced as
\cite[Theorem 3.1]{xl17}, where a $\mathrm{Hom}$-Lie structure is written as its matrix in the standard
basis $\{X,Y,H\}=\{e,f,h\}$ of $\mathfrak{sl}_2$:
$$\mathcal{H}(\mathfrak{sl}_2)=\langle E_{12},\ E_{21},\ E_{33},\ E_{11}+E_{22},\ 2E_{13}+E_{32},\
2E_{23}+E_{31}\rangle .$$
This is exactly the space described above: the six listed matrices correspond, in the
parametrization of Theorem \ref{thm:sl2}, to $c_2=1$, $b_3=1$, $a_1=1$, $b_2=c_3=1$,
$(a_2,c_1)=(2,1)$ and $(a_3,b_1)=(2,1)$ respectively, and conversely the relations $b_2=c_3$,
$a_2=2c_1$, $a_3=2b_1$ say precisely that the matrix of $\varphi$ lies in their span.  We keep
the statement here because it follows from Corollary \ref{cor:triples} by a short computation,
which is independent of the structure theory of semi-simple Lie algebras, and it
is valid over an arbitrary field of characteristic zero (algebraic closedness, assumed in
\cite{xjl15,xl17}, is not needed); it also shows that the general lower bound of Theorem
\ref{thm:dim3} is sharp.
<!-- end remark-8 -->
<!-- corollary-5: body_md -->
\label{cor:sl2tp}
Every transposed Poisson structure on $\mathfrak{sl}_2$ is trivial, while $\mathfrak{sl}_2$ admits non-trivial
$\mathrm{Hom}$-Lie structures.  In particular the implication of Proposition \ref{prop:homtr} cannot be
reversed.
<!-- end corollary-5 -->
<!-- remark-9: body_md -->
\label{rem:sl2tpfkl}
The first assertion of Corollary \ref{cor:sl2tp} is not a new result: it is the special case
$\mathfrak{L}=\mathfrak{sl}_2$ of \cite[Corollary 9]{FKL21}, where Ferreira, Kaygorodov and Lopatkin prove that a
complex semi-simple finite-dimensional Lie algebra admits no non-trivial transposed Poisson
structure.  Their argument combines \cite[Theorem 8]{FKL21} --- a Lie algebra all of whose
$\frac12$-derivations are trivial carries only trivial transposed Poisson structures --- with
Filippov's description of the $\frac12$-derivations of simple finite-dimensional Lie algebras
(see \cite{FKL21,K07}).  The derivation of Corollary \ref{cor:sl2tp} from Theorem
\ref{thm:sl2} is self-contained, does not use the structure theory of semi-simple Lie algebras, and is valid over
an arbitrary field of characteristic zero, whereas \cite{FKL21} works over $\mathbb{C}$.  What is
relevant for the present paper is the combination of this known fact with the second assertion:
$\mathfrak{sl}_2$ has a $6$-dimensional space of $\mathrm{Hom}$-Lie structures by Theorem \ref{thm:sl2}, so it
witnesses that the implication of Proposition \ref{prop:homtr} is strict.
<!-- end remark-9 -->
<!-- remark-10: body_md -->
\label{rem:sl2dim}
On $\mathfrak{sl}_2$ the trivial $\mathrm{Hom}$-Lie structures $\varphi=\alpha\,\mathrm{id}$ form a $1$-dimensional
subspace of the $6$-dimensional space of all $\mathrm{Hom}$-Lie structures, so the bound of Theorem
\ref{thm:dim3} is sharp.  By contrast, on the three-dimensional Heisenberg algebra the space of
$\mathrm{Hom}$-Lie structures is the whole $9$-dimensional space $\mathrm{End}(\mathfrak{L})$, by Proposition
\ref{prop:2step}.  Both extremes allowed by Theorem \ref{thm:dim3} therefore occur.
<!-- end remark-10 -->
<!-- theorem-6: body_md -->
\label{thm:dim3exact}
Let $\mathfrak{L}$ be a three-dimensional Lie algebra over an arbitrary field.  Then the space
$\mathcal{H}(\mathfrak{L})$ of $\mathrm{Hom}$-Lie structures of $\mathfrak{L}$ has codimension exactly $\dim \mathfrak{L}^3$ in
$\mathrm{End}(\mathfrak{L})$; that is,
$$\dim \mathcal{H}(\mathfrak{L})=9-\dim \mathfrak{L}^3, \qquad \mathfrak{L}^3=[\mathfrak{L},[\mathfrak{L},\mathfrak{L}]] .$$
<!-- end theorem-6 -->
<!-- corollary-6: body_md -->
\label{cor:dim3list}
Let $\mathfrak{L}$ be a three-dimensional Lie algebra over an algebraically closed field $\mathbb{F}$ of
characteristic zero.  Then $\dim \mathcal{H}(\mathfrak{L})$ is given by the following table, in which the
algebras are listed in the standard classification and only the non-zero brackets of basis
vectors are displayed.
$$\begin{array}{llcc}
\text{algebra} & \text{multiplication} & \dim \mathfrak{L}^3 & \dim \mathcal{H}(\mathfrak{L})\\[2pt]
\hline
A_3 \ \text{(abelian)} & - & 0 & 9\\
\mathfrak{N}_3 \ \text{(Heisenberg)} & [e_1,e_2]=e_3 & 0 & 9\\
\mathfrak{r}_2 \oplus \mathbb{F} & [e_1,e_2]=e_2 & 1 & 8\\
\mathfrak{r}_3 & [e_1,e_2]=e_2,\ [e_1,e_3]=e_2+e_3 & 2 & 7\\
\mathfrak{r}_{3,\lambda} \ (\lambda \neq 0) & [e_1,e_2]=e_2,\ [e_1,e_3]=\lambda e_3 & 2 & 7\\
\mathfrak{sl}_2 & [h,e]=2e,\ [h,f]=-2f,\ [e,f]=h & 3 & 6
\end{array}$$
In particular every three-dimensional Lie algebra admits non-trivial $\mathrm{Hom}$-Lie structures, the
value $9$ is attained exactly on the two-step nilpotent algebras, and the minimum $6$ is attained
exactly on $\mathfrak{sl}_2$.
<!-- end corollary-6 -->
<!-- remark-11: body_md -->
\label{rem:dim3tp}
Corollary \ref{cor:dim3list} is the $\mathrm{Hom}$-Lie counterpart of the classification of the
three-dimensional transposed Poisson algebras obtained by Beites, Fern\'andez Ouaridi and
Kaygorodov \cite{BFOK}.  The two pictures are quite different: the transposed Poisson structures
of a three-dimensional Lie algebra may well be all trivial --- this is the case for $\mathfrak{sl}_2$ by
Corollary \ref{cor:sl2tp} --- while the space of $\mathrm{Hom}$-Lie structures is never smaller than
$6$-dimensional.  Theorem \ref{thm:dim3exact} also shows that in dimension three the
dimension of $\mathcal{H}(\mathfrak{L})$ is determined by the single number $\dim \mathfrak{L}^3$; in particular
it is the same, namely $7$, for all the algebras $\mathfrak{r}_{3,\lambda}$ with
$\lambda \neq 0$ and for $\mathfrak{r}_3$.
<!-- end remark-11 -->
<!-- definition-5: body_md -->
\label{def:osc}
The oscillator Lie algebra $\mathfrak{L}_{\lambda}$ is the $(2n+2)$-dimensional real Lie algebra with
canonical basis $\mathbb{B}=\{e_{-1},e_0,e_i,f_i\}_{i=1,\ldots,n}$ and multiplication
$$[e_{-1},e_i]=\lambda_i f_i, \qquad [e_{-1},f_i]=-\lambda_i e_i, \qquad [e_i,f_i]=e_0
\qquad (i=1,\ldots,n),$$
where $\lambda=(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_n) \in \mathbb{R}^n$ with
$0<\lambda_1 \leq \ldots \leq \lambda_n$; all the remaining brackets of basis elements vanish.
<!-- end definition-5 -->
<!-- theorem-7: body_md -->
\label{thm:osc}
Let $\mathfrak{L}_{\lambda}$ be the $(2n+2)$-dimensional oscillator Lie algebra, $n \geq 1$, and let
$\varphi$ be a linear map on $\mathfrak{L}_{\lambda}$.  Then $\varphi$ is a $\mathrm{Hom}$-Lie structure if and
only if it has the form
\begin{align*}
\varphi(e_i) &= \sum_{j=1}^{n}\alpha_{j,i}e_j+\sum_{j=1}^{n}\beta_{j,i}f_j+\delta_i e_0
  && (i=1,\ldots,n),\\
\varphi(f_i) &= \sum_{j=1}^{n}\xi_{j,i}e_j+\sum_{j=1}^{n}\eta_{j,i}f_j+\tau_i e_0
  && (i=1,\ldots,n),\\
\varphi(e_{-1}) &= \sum_{j=1}^{n}\alpha_{j,-1}e_j+\sum_{j=1}^{n}\beta_{j,-1}f_j
  +\gamma_{-1}e_{-1}+\delta_{-1}e_0, &&\\
\varphi(e_0) &= \delta_0 e_0, &&
\end{align*}
where the coefficients satisfy
$$\alpha_{j,i}=\frac{\lambda_i}{\lambda_j}\alpha_{i,j}, \qquad
\beta_{j,i}=\frac{\lambda_i}{\lambda_j}\xi_{i,j}, \qquad
\eta_{j,i}=\frac{\lambda_i}{\lambda_j}\eta_{i,j}, \qquad 1 \leq i,j \leq n,$$
and the coefficients $\delta_i$, $\tau_i$, $\delta_0$, $\gamma_{-1}$, $\alpha_{j,-1}$,
$\beta_{j,-1}$, $\delta_{-1}$ are arbitrary.
<!-- end theorem-7 -->
<!-- remark-12: body_md -->
\label{rem:osc}
The second relation of Theorem \ref{thm:osc} couples $\beta$ with $\xi$ and not, as the symmetry
of the first and third relations might suggest, with $\eta$: the triple $\{e_i,f_k,e_{-1}\}$
produces $\lambda_i\xi_{i,k}=\lambda_k\beta_{k,i}$, because $[\varphi(e_i),e_k]$ picks out the
$f$-component of $\varphi(e_i)$ while $[\varphi(f_k),f_i]$ picks out its $e$-component.  No
relation of the form $\beta_{j,i}=\frac{\lambda_i}{\lambda_j}\eta_{i,j}$ holds: for $n=1$ and
$\lambda_1=1$, the map $\varphi(e_1)=f_1$, $\varphi(f_1)=e_1$, $\varphi(e_{-1})=\varphi(e_0)=0$
satisfies the conditions of Theorem \ref{thm:osc} (here $\beta_{1,1}=\xi_{1,1}=1$ and
$\alpha_{1,1}=\eta_{1,1}=0$), so it is a $\mathrm{Hom}$-Lie structure, but $\beta_{1,1} \neq \eta_{1,1}$.
<!-- end remark-12 -->
<!-- definition-6: body_md -->
\label{def:codim1}
Let $\mathfrak{L}$ be the solvable Lie algebra with abelian nilpotent radical
$\mathfrak{N}=\langle e_i \rangle_{i \geq 2}$ of codimension $1$, spanned by the generators
$\{e_i\}_{i \in \mathbb{N}}$ and subject to
$$[e_1,e_n]=e_n, \qquad n \geq 2 ,$$
all the remaining brackets of basis elements being zero.
<!-- end definition-6 -->
<!-- theorem-8: body_md -->
\label{thm:codim1}
Let $\mathfrak{L}$ be a solvable Lie algebra with abelian nilpotent radical $\mathfrak{N}$ of codimension $1$, and
assume $\dim \mathfrak{N} \geq 2$, which is the case in Definition \ref{def:codim1}.  Then a linear map
$\varphi$ on $\mathfrak{L}$ is a $\mathrm{Hom}$-Lie structure if and only if $\varphi$ preserves the radical,
$\varphi(\mathfrak{N}) \subseteq \mathfrak{N}$.  In the basis of Definition \ref{def:codim1} this reads
$$\varphi(e_1)=\sum_{i \in \mathbb{N}}\alpha_{1,i}e_i, \qquad
\varphi(e_j)=\sum_{i \geq 2}\alpha_{j,i}e_i \quad (j>1),$$
the value $\varphi(e_1)$ being arbitrary.
<!-- end theorem-8 -->
<!-- definition-7: body_md -->
\label{def:witt}
Let $\mathfrak{W}$ be the Witt algebra, i.e. the Lie algebra with basis $\{e_i\}_{i \in \mathbb{Z}}$ and
multiplication $[e_i,e_j]=(i-j)e_{i+j}$.
<!-- end definition-7 -->
<!-- theorem-9: body_md -->
\label{thm:witt}
Let $\mathfrak{W}$ be the Witt algebra and let $\varphi$ be a linear map on $\mathfrak{W}$.  Then $\varphi$ is a
$\mathrm{Hom}$-Lie structure if and only if
$$\varphi(e_i)=\sum_{j \in \mathbb{Z}}\alpha_j e_{i+j}, \qquad i \in \mathbb{Z},$$
where only finitely many of the coefficients $\alpha_j$ are non-zero and, crucially, they do not
depend on $i$.  Equivalently, writing $\gamma=\alpha_0$,
$$\varphi(e_i)=\sum_{j \in \mathbb{Z} \setminus \{0\}}\alpha_j e_{i+j}+\gamma e_i, \qquad i \in \mathbb{Z} .$$
<!-- end theorem-9 -->
<!-- remark-13: body_md -->
\label{rem:wittknown}
Theorem \ref{thm:witt} is not a new result: it is \cite[Theorem 3.2]{xl17}.  There the algebra
$\mathfrak{W}$ is called the Virasoro algebra --- it is the centreless Virasoro algebra, with basis
$\{L_n\}_{n \in \mathbb{Z}}$ and $[L_m,L_n]=(m-n)L_{m+n}$, i.e. our Witt algebra of Definition
\ref{def:witt} --- and the answer is stated in the form
$$\mathcal{H}(\mathfrak{W})=\bigoplus_{i \in \mathbb{Z}}\mathbb{F}\sigma_i, \qquad \sigma_i(L_n)=L_{n+i} ,$$
which is exactly the description above: a finite linear combination $\sum_i \alpha_i \sigma_i$
is precisely a map $e_n \mapsto \sum_i \alpha_i e_{n+i}$ with finitely many non-zero
coefficients $\alpha_i$ not depending on $n$.  This is also the case of the ``two-sided Witt
algebra'' recorded in the introduction of \cite{MZ18}.  The proof in \cite{xl17} proceeds by
showing that $\mathcal{H}(\mathfrak{W})$ is graded (the algebra possesses a finite commutant generating
set) and then treating the homogeneous components separately; our approach is a direct
computation with the identity (\ref{HOM}), and Theorem \ref{thm:witt} is valid over an arbitrary
field of characteristic zero (algebraic closedness, assumed in \cite{xl17}, is not used).
<!-- end remark-13 -->
<!-- remark-14: body_md -->
\label{rem:witt}
The independence of the coefficients $\alpha_j$ from $i$ is essential, and it is not implied by
the triples $\{e_0,e_i,e_j\}$ alone.  Indeed, those triples, evaluated on the specializations
$m=i-j$, $m=j-i$ and $m=0$, yield the relations
$$\alpha_{i,j}=\alpha_{0,j-i} \ \ (i \neq j), \qquad
\alpha_{i,i}=(i+1)\alpha_{0,0}-i\alpha_{1,1} \ \ (i \neq 1),$$
which would allow the diagonal coefficient to be $\gamma$ at $i=1$ and $(i+1)\beta-\gamma$ at
$i \neq 1$.  Such maps are not $\mathrm{Hom}$-Lie structures when $\beta \neq 0$.  For instance, let
$\beta=1$, $\gamma=0$ and $\alpha_j=0$ for all $j$, so that $\varphi(e_1)=0$ and
$\varphi(e_i)=(i+1)e_i$ for $i \neq 1$.  Then the triple $\{e_0,e_2,e_3\}$ gives
\begin{align*}
E_{\varphi}(e_0,e_2,e_3)
&=[\varphi(e_0),[e_2,e_3]]+[\varphi(e_2),[e_3,e_0]]+[\varphi(e_3),[e_0,e_2]]\\
&=[e_0,-e_5]+[3e_2,3e_3]+[4e_3,-2e_2]
=5e_5-9e_5-8e_5=-12\,e_5 \neq 0 .
\end{align*}
The triples $\{e_k,e_i,e_j\}$ with $k \neq 0$ thus impose genuinely stronger conditions, and by
Theorem \ref{thm:witt} they force $\beta=0$: no $\mathrm{Hom}$-Lie structure of the Witt algebra has a
diagonal coefficient depending on $i$.
<!-- end remark-14 -->
<!-- definition-8: body_md -->
\label{def:vir}
Let $\mathfrak{V}$ be the Virasoro algebra, i.e. the Lie algebra with basis
$\{e_i\}_{i \in \mathbb{Z}} \cup \{c\}$ and multiplication
$$[e_i,e_j]=(i-j)e_{i+j}+\delta_{i+j,0}\,\frac{i^3-i}{12}\,c, \qquad [e_i,c]=[c,e_i]=0 .$$
<!-- end definition-8 -->
<!-- theorem-10: body_md -->
\label{thm:vir}
Let $\mathfrak{V}$ be the Virasoro algebra and let $\varphi$ be a linear map on $\mathfrak{V}$.  Then $\varphi$ is a
$\mathrm{Hom}$-Lie structure if and only if there are a scalar $\alpha \in \mathbb{F}$ and a linear form
$f \colon \mathfrak{V} \to \mathbb{F}$ such that
$$\varphi(x)=\alpha x+f(x)\,c \qquad \text{for all } x \in \mathfrak{V},$$
that is, if and only if $\varphi$ is a scalar multiple of the identity modulo the centre.
<!-- end theorem-10 -->
<!-- remark-15: body_md -->
\label{rem:vir}
The contrast with the Witt algebra is sharp.  The shift $\varphi(e_i)=e_{i+1}$ is a $\mathrm{Hom}$-Lie
structure of the Witt algebra by Theorem \ref{thm:witt} (take $\alpha_1=1$ and $\alpha_j=0$ for
$j \neq 1$), but the map $\varphi(e_i)=e_{i+1}$, $\varphi(c)=0$ is \emph{not} a $\mathrm{Hom}$-Lie
structure of the Virasoro algebra, by Theorem \ref{thm:vir}, since it is not scalar modulo the
centre.  It is exactly the central term $\delta_{i+j,0}\frac{i^3-i}{12}c$ of the Virasoro bracket
that rules out all the shifts $\alpha_j$ with $j \neq 0$.
<!-- end remark-15 -->
<!-- remark-16: body_md -->
\label{rem:virkm}
Theorem \ref{thm:vir} should be compared with \cite[Theorem 3]{MZ18}, which states that the
space of $\mathrm{Hom}$-Lie structures on an affine Kac--Moody algebra $\widehat{\mathfrak{g}}$ is
linearly spanned by the identity map and by the $\mathrm{Hom}$-Lie structures with central image, i.e.
by the maps $\widehat{\mathfrak{g}}\to \mathbb{F} z$.  This is formally the same answer as the one
obtained here for the Virasoro algebra: $\varphi=\alpha\,\mathrm{id}+f(\cdot)c$.  The Virasoro algebra
is, however, not an affine Kac--Moody algebra --- it is the universal central extension of the
Witt algebra, not of a loop algebra --- and we have not found the Virasoro case stated in
\cite{MZ18}, whose Sections 4 and 5 treat the untwisted and the twisted affine Kac--Moody algebras.
Theorem \ref{thm:vir} is therefore the exact analogue of \cite[Theorem 3]{MZ18} for the
Virasoro algebra, proved here independently.  The mechanism behind the two results is the same,
and it is the one isolated in Lemma \ref{lem:clift} below: on the centreless algebra there is a
large supply of $\mathrm{Hom}$-Lie structures (Theorem \ref{thm:witt} for the Witt algebra), and passing
to a central extension all of them except the scalar ones are killed by the obstruction coming
from the defining $2$-cocycle.
<!-- end remark-16 -->
<!-- corollary-7: body_md -->
\label{cor:virtp}
The Virasoro algebra admits no non-zero transposed Poisson structure.
<!-- end corollary-7 -->
<!-- definition-9: body_md -->
\label{def:hv}
Let $\mathfrak{HV}=W(0,0)$ be the (centreless) Heisenberg--Virasoro algebra, i.e. the semidirect product of
the Witt algebra with an abelian ideal: it has basis
$\{L_i\}_{i \in \mathbb{Z}} \cup \{I_i\}_{i \in \mathbb{Z}}$ and multiplication
$$[L_i,L_j]=(i-j)L_{i+j}, \qquad [L_i,I_j]=-j\,I_{i+j}, \qquad [I_i,I_j]=0 .$$
<!-- end definition-9 -->
<!-- theorem-11: body_md -->
\label{thm:hv}
For $t \in \mathbb{Z}$ let $\psi_t$ be the linear map on $\mathfrak{HV}$ with $\psi_t(L_i)=I_{i+t}$ and
$\psi_t(I_k)=0$.  Then $\psi_t$ is a $\mathrm{Hom}$-Lie structure of $\mathfrak{HV}$, and hence so is every map
$$\varphi=\alpha\,\mathrm{id}+\sum_{t \in S}q_t\psi_t+f(\cdot)\,I_0$$
with $\alpha, q_t \in \mathbb{F}$, $S \subseteq \mathbb{Z}$ finite and $f$ an arbitrary linear form on $\mathfrak{HV}$.
<!-- end theorem-11 -->
<!-- remark-17: body_md -->
\label{rem:hv}
As for the Virasoro algebra (Remark \ref{rem:vir}), the shifts of the Witt algebra do not survive:
the map $\varphi(L_i)=L_{i+1}$, $\varphi(I_k)=0$ is \emph{not} a $\mathrm{Hom}$-Lie structure of $\mathfrak{HV}$.
Indeed, for the triple $(L_1,L_0,I_1)$,
\begin{align*}
E_{\varphi}(L_1,L_0,I_1)&=[L_2,[L_0,I_1]]+[L_1,[I_1,L_1]]+[0,[L_1,L_0]]\\
&=[L_2,-I_1]+[L_1,I_2]=I_3-2I_3=-I_3 \neq 0 .
\end{align*}
So only the ``vertical'' shifts $\psi_t$ of Theorem \ref{thm:hv}, which move the Witt part
\emph{into} the abelian ideal, remain.
<!-- end remark-17 -->
<!-- definition-10: body_md -->
\label{def:wab}
Let $\Gamma$ be a non-trivial additive subgroup of $\mathbb{F}$ and let $a,b \in \mathbb{F}$.  The Lie algebra
$W(\Gamma;a,b)$ has basis $\{L_{\mu}\}_{\mu \in \Gamma} \cup \{I_{\mu}\}_{\mu \in \Gamma}$ and
multiplication
$$[L_{\mu},L_{\nu}]=(\mu-\nu)L_{\mu+\nu}, \qquad
[L_{\mu},I_{\nu}]=-(\nu+b\mu+a)I_{\mu+\nu}, \qquad [I_{\mu},I_{\nu}]=0 .$$
For $\Gamma=\mathbb{Z}$ this is the algebra $W(a,b)=\mathfrak{W} \ltimes A_{a,b}$; thus
$W(\mathbb{Z};0,0)=\mathfrak{HV}$ is the Heisenberg--Virasoro algebra of Definition \ref{def:hv}, and the
$L$-part is always a copy of the Witt algebra $\mathfrak{W}$ (of the higher rank Witt algebra
$W(\Gamma)$ in general).
<!-- end definition-10 -->
<!-- remark-18: body_md -->
\label{rem:wabdghv}
Two further families of the literature are members of this one.  The algebras
$\mathcal{W}(a,b)$ of \cite{KKhS25} are $W(\mathbb{Z};a,b)$.  The centreless deformed generalized
Heisenberg--Virasoro algebra $\check{g}(G,\lambda)$ of \cite{KKhS24b}, with
$[L_{\mu},L_{\nu}]=(\nu-\mu)L_{\mu+\nu}$ and $[L_{\mu},I_{\nu}]=(\nu-\lambda\mu)I_{\mu+\nu}$,
becomes $W(G;0,-\lambda)$ after the substitution $L_{\mu}\mapsto -L_{\mu}$.
<!-- end remark-18 -->
<!-- definition-11: body_md -->
\label{def:wabshift}
For $t \in \Gamma$ and $\alpha,\beta,\gamma \in \mathbb{F}$ let $\varphi_{t;\alpha,\beta,\gamma}$ be the
\emph{graded shift} of degree $t$ determined by
$$\varphi_{t;\alpha,\beta,\gamma}(L_{\mu})=\alpha L_{\mu+t}+\beta I_{\mu+t}, \qquad
\varphi_{t;\alpha,\beta,\gamma}(I_{\mu})=\gamma I_{\mu+t} \qquad (\mu \in \Gamma).$$
<!-- end definition-11 -->
<!-- theorem-12: body_md -->
\label{thm:wab}
Let $\Gamma$ be a non-trivial additive subgroup of $\mathbb{F}$ and let $a,b \in \mathbb{F}$, $t \in \Gamma$,
$\alpha,\beta,\gamma \in \mathbb{F}$.  Then $\varphi_{t;\alpha,\beta,\gamma}$ is a $\mathrm{Hom}$-Lie structure
of $W(\Gamma;a,b)$ if and only if
$$\gamma=\alpha \qquad \text{and} \qquad \alpha\,t\,(b^2-1)=0 .$$
In particular the coefficient $\beta$ is arbitrary.
<!-- end theorem-12 -->
<!-- corollary-8: body_md -->
\label{cor:wabpsi}
For all $t \in \Gamma$ and $\beta \in \mathbb{F}$ the map
$$\psi_{t,\beta} \colon \quad L_{\mu} \mapsto \beta I_{\mu+t}, \qquad I_{\mu}\mapsto 0$$
is a $\mathrm{Hom}$-Lie structure of $W(\Gamma;a,b)$.  Consequently every map
$$\varphi=\alpha\,\mathrm{id}+\sum_{t \in S}\psi_{t,\beta_t}, \qquad S \subseteq \Gamma \ \text{finite},$$
is a $\mathrm{Hom}$-Lie structure, so $\mathcal{H}(W(\Gamma;a,b))$ is infinite-dimensional for every
$a,b$ whenever $\Gamma$ is infinite.
<!-- end corollary-8 -->
<!-- corollary-9: body_md -->
\label{cor:wabcases}
Let $t \in \Gamma$, $t \neq 0$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item If $b=1$ or $b=-1$, then $\varphi_{t;\alpha,\beta,\alpha}$ is a $\mathrm{Hom}$-Lie structure of
$W(\Gamma;a,b)$ for all $\alpha,\beta$.
\item If $b^2 \neq 1$, then the only graded shifts of non-zero degree that are $\mathrm{Hom}$-Lie
structures are the maps $\psi_{t,\beta}$ of Corollary \ref{cor:wabpsi}, whose $L$-part lands
inside the abelian ideal.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end corollary-9 -->
<!-- remark-19: body_md -->
\label{rem:wabhv}
For $(a,b)=(0,0)$ and $\Gamma=\mathbb{Z}$ we have $b^2-1=-1 \neq 0$, so Corollary \ref{cor:wabcases}(2)
recovers Theorem \ref{thm:hv} together with Remark \ref{rem:hv}: the maps $\psi_t=\psi_{t,1}$ are
$\mathrm{Hom}$-Lie structures of $\mathfrak{HV}$, and the Witt-type shift $L_i \mapsto L_{i+1}$, $I_k \mapsto 0$
is not.
<!-- end remark-19 -->
<!-- remark-20: body_md -->
\label{rem:wabhalf}
By \cite{KKhS25} the algebra $\mathcal{W}(a,b)=W(\mathbb{Z};a,b)$ has non-trivial
$\frac12$-derivations only for $b=-1$.  Theorem \ref{thm:wab} shows that the $\mathrm{Hom}$-Lie picture
is completely different: the maps $\psi_{t,\beta}$ exist for \emph{all} values of $a$ and $b$, so
that $\Delta(W(\mathbb{Z};a,b))=\langle \mathrm{id} \rangle$ while $\mathcal{H}(W(\mathbb{Z};a,b))$ is
infinite-dimensional; moreover, non-trivial \emph{Witt-type} shifts survive not only for $b=-1$,
but also for $b=1$.  This is the announced strengthening of Remark \ref{rem:halfstrict}.
<!-- end remark-20 -->
<!-- definition-12: body_md -->
\label{def:schro}
Let $\Gamma$ be a non-trivial additive subgroup of $\mathbb{F}$ and let $a,b \in \mathbb{F}$.  The
\emph{deformative Schr\"odinger--Witt algebra} $\mathcal{S}(\Gamma;a,b)$ has basis
$\{L_{\mu}\}\cup\{I_{\mu}\}\cup\{Y_{\mu}\}$, $\mu \in \Gamma$, and multiplication
\begin{align*}
[L_{\mu},L_{\nu}]&=(\nu-\mu)L_{\mu+\nu}, &
[L_{\mu},I_{\nu}]&=(\nu+b\mu+a)I_{\mu+\nu}, \\
[L_{\mu},Y_{\nu}]&=\Big(\nu+\tfrac{(b-1)\mu+a}{2}\Big)Y_{\mu+\nu}, &
[Y_{\mu},Y_{\nu}]&=(\nu-\mu)I_{\mu+\nu},
\end{align*}
all other brackets of basis vectors being zero.
<!-- end definition-12 -->
<!-- definition-13: body_md -->
\label{def:schroshift}
For $t \in \Gamma$ and $\alpha,\beta,\gamma,\delta \in \mathbb{F}$ let
$\varphi_{t;\alpha,\beta,\gamma,\delta}$ be the graded shift of degree $t$ with
$$L_{\mu}\mapsto \alpha L_{\mu+t}+\beta I_{\mu+t}, \qquad
I_{\mu}\mapsto \gamma I_{\mu+t}, \qquad Y_{\mu}\mapsto \delta Y_{\mu+t}.$$
<!-- end definition-13 -->
<!-- theorem-13: body_md -->
\label{thm:schro}
Let $\Gamma$ be a non-trivial additive subgroup of $\mathbb{F}$, $a,b \in \mathbb{F}$, $t \in \Gamma$ and
$\alpha,\beta,\gamma,\delta \in \mathbb{F}$.  Then $\varphi_{t;\alpha,\beta,\gamma,\delta}$ is a
$\mathrm{Hom}$-Lie structure of $\mathcal{S}(\Gamma;a,b)$ if and only if
$$\gamma=\delta=\alpha \qquad \text{and} \qquad \alpha\,t\,(b+1)=0 .$$
<!-- end theorem-13 -->
<!-- corollary-10: body_md -->
\label{cor:schropsi}
For all $t \in \Gamma$ and $\beta \in \mathbb{F}$ the map
$L_{\mu}\mapsto \beta I_{\mu+t}$, $I_{\mu}\mapsto 0$, $Y_{\mu}\mapsto 0$ is a $\mathrm{Hom}$-Lie
structure of $\mathcal{S}(\Gamma;a,b)$, for all values of $a$ and $b$.  Hence
$\mathcal{H}(\mathcal{S}(\Gamma;a,b))$ is infinite-dimensional whenever $\Gamma$ is infinite.
<!-- end corollary-10 -->
<!-- remark-21: body_md -->
\label{rem:schrohalf}
By Theorem \ref{thm:schro} a graded shift with a non-zero Witt part and non-zero degree exists
exactly when $b=-1$ --- which is precisely the condition under which $\mathcal{W}(a,b,s)$ has
non-trivial $\frac12$-derivations, and hence non-trivial transposed Poisson structures, by
\cite{KKhS24a}.  In terms of the parameters of \cite{Sh24}, the algebra $L_{\lambda,\mu}$ is
exceptional exactly for $\lambda=1$.  Note, however, that even in the non-exceptional cases the
algebras carry the infinite family of $\mathrm{Hom}$-Lie structures of Corollary \ref{cor:schropsi}.
<!-- end remark-21 -->
<!-- definition-14: body_md -->
\label{def:eschro}
The \emph{extended Schr\"odinger--Witt algebra} $\widetilde{\mathfrak{so}}$ has basis
$\{L_n,M_n,N_n\}_{n \in \mathbb{Z}}\cup\{Y_{n+\frac12}\}_{n \in \mathbb{Z}}$ and multiplication
\begin{align*}
[L_m,L_n]&=(n-m)L_{m+n}, & [L_m,M_n]&=nM_{m+n}, & [L_m,N_n]&=nN_{m+n},\\
[N_m,M_n]&=2M_{m+n}, & [N_m,Y_{n+\frac12}]&=Y_{m+n+\frac12}, &
[Y_{m+\frac12},Y_{n+\frac12}]&=(m-n)M_{m+n+1},
\end{align*}
together with $[L_m,Y_{n+\frac12}]=\big(n+\frac{1-m}{2}\big)Y_{m+n+\frac12}$; all remaining
brackets of basis vectors vanish.
<!-- end definition-14 -->
<!-- theorem-14: body_md -->
\label{thm:eschro}
For every $t \in \mathbb{Z}$ and every $\beta \in \mathbb{F}$ the linear map $\chi_{t,\beta}$ determined by
$$\chi_{t,\beta}(L_m)=\beta M_{m+t}, \qquad
\chi_{t,\beta}(M_n)=\chi_{t,\beta}(N_n)=\chi_{t,\beta}(Y_{n+\frac12})=0$$
is a $\mathrm{Hom}$-Lie structure of $\widetilde{\mathfrak{so}}$.  Consequently
$$\alpha\,\mathrm{id}+\sum_{t \in S}\chi_{t,\beta_t}, \qquad S \subseteq \mathbb{Z} \ \text{finite},$$
is a $\mathrm{Hom}$-Lie structure for all $\alpha,\beta_t \in \mathbb{F}$, and
$\mathcal{H}(\widetilde{\mathfrak{so}})$ is infinite-dimensional.
<!-- end theorem-14 -->
<!-- remark-22: body_md -->
\label{rem:eschro}
By \cite{Sh24} every $\frac12$-derivation of $\widetilde{\mathfrak{so}}$ is trivial, so that
$\widetilde{\mathfrak{so}}$ carries no non-trivial transposed Poisson structure.  Theorem
\ref{thm:eschro} therefore provides a particularly striking illustration of
Remark \ref{rem:halfstrict}: here $\Delta(\widetilde{\mathfrak{so}})=\langle \mathrm{id} \rangle$ is
one-dimensional while $\mathcal{H}(\widetilde{\mathfrak{so}})$ is infinite-dimensional.  It also
shows that the converse of Proposition \ref{prop:homtr} fails for infinite-dimensional algebras
as badly as it does for $\mathfrak{sl}_2$.
<!-- end remark-22 -->
<!-- definition-15: body_md -->
\label{def:wng}
Let $G$ be a non-trivial additive subgroup of $\mathbb{F}$ and let $n \in \mathbb{Z}$.  The
\emph{not-finitely graded Witt algebra} $W_n(G)$ has basis
$\{L_{\alpha,i}\}_{\alpha \in G,\, i \in \mathbb{Z}}$ and multiplication
$$[L_{\alpha,i},L_{\beta,j}]=(\beta-\alpha)L_{\alpha+\beta,i+j}+(j-i)L_{\alpha+\beta,i+j+n}.$$
The \emph{not-finitely graded Heisenberg--Witt algebra} $HW_n(G)$ has basis
$\{L_{\alpha,i},H_{\alpha,i}\}_{\alpha \in G,\, i \in \mathbb{Z}}$, the same bracket on the $L$'s, and
$$[L_{\alpha,i},H_{\beta,j}]=\beta H_{\alpha+\beta,i+j}+jH_{\alpha+\beta,i+j+n}, \qquad
[H_{\alpha,i},H_{\beta,j}]=0 .$$
<!-- end definition-15 -->
<!-- theorem-15: body_md -->
\label{thm:wng}
For all $d \in G$, $m \in \mathbb{Z}$ and $c \in \mathbb{F}$ the graded shift
$$\sigma_{d,m,c} \colon \quad L_{\alpha,i}\longmapsto c\,L_{\alpha+d,i+m}$$
is a $\mathrm{Hom}$-Lie structure of $W_n(G)$.  Consequently every translation invariant map
$$\varphi(L_{\alpha,i})=\sum_{d \in G,\ m \in \mathbb{Z}}c_{d,m}\,L_{\alpha+d,i+m}$$
with finitely many non-zero coefficients $c_{d,m}$, independent of $(\alpha,i)$, is a $\mathrm{Hom}$-Lie
structure of $W_n(G)$.
<!-- end theorem-15 -->
<!-- theorem-16: body_md -->
\label{thm:hwng}
Let $G$ be a non-trivial additive subgroup of $\mathbb{F}$, let $n \in \mathbb{Z}$, $d \in G$, $m \in \mathbb{Z}$ and
$\alpha,\beta,\gamma \in \mathbb{F}$, and let $\varphi$ be the graded shift of $HW_n(G)$ determined by
$$L_{\alpha_0,i}\mapsto \alpha L_{\alpha_0+d,i+m}+\beta H_{\alpha_0+d,i+m}, \qquad
H_{\alpha_0,i}\mapsto \gamma H_{\alpha_0+d,i+m}.$$
\begin{enumerate}
\item If $\gamma=\alpha$, $\gamma d=0$ and $\gamma m=0$, then $\varphi$ is a $\mathrm{Hom}$-Lie structure.
In particular $L_{\alpha_0,i}\mapsto \beta H_{\alpha_0+d,i+m}$, $H_{\alpha_0,i}\mapsto 0$ is a
$\mathrm{Hom}$-Lie structure for every shift $(d,m)$ and every $\beta$.
\item Conversely, if $n \neq 0$ and $\varphi$ is a $\mathrm{Hom}$-Lie structure with $\alpha=\gamma$,
then $\gamma d=0$ and $\gamma m=0$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end theorem-16 -->
<!-- remark-23: body_md -->
\label{rem:hwng}
For $n=0$ the condition for the graded shift $\varphi$ of Theorem \ref{thm:hwng} to be a
$\mathrm{Hom}$-Lie structure becomes $\alpha=\gamma$ and $\gamma(d+m)=0$; the surviving shifts are then those with $d \in G \cap \mathbb{Z}$
and $m=-d$.  This matches exactly the description of $\Delta(HW_0(G))$ obtained in
\cite{KKhS24a}.
<!-- end remark-23 -->
<!-- remark-24: body_md -->
\label{rem:nfgcentral}
The algebras $\widehat{W}(G)$, $\widetilde{W}(G)$ and $\widetilde{HW}(G)$ of \cite{KKhS24b} are
central extensions of $W_1(G)$, $W_{-1}(G)$ and of a Heisenberg--Witt algebra.  As the passage
from the Witt algebra to the Virasoro algebra shows (Theorem \ref{thm:vir} and Remark
\ref{rem:vir}), a central term of the bracket can destroy all the graded shifts of Theorem
\ref{thm:wng}; this is settled in Section \ref{sec:nfgc}, where it turns out that the graded
shifts survive in $\widehat{W}(G)$ exactly when they move the second index upwards (Theorem
\ref{thm:hatw}), and that all the non-trivial ones die in $\widetilde{W}(G)$ (Theorem
\ref{thm:tildew}).
<!-- end remark-24 -->
<!-- definition-16: body_md -->
\label{def:cext}
Let $(\mathfrak{L},[\cdot,\cdot]_0)$ be a Lie algebra, let $Z$ be a vector space and let
$\omega \colon \mathfrak{L} \times \mathfrak{L} \to Z$ be an alternating bilinear map satisfying the cocycle
identity
\begin{equation}\label{cocycle}
\omega([x,y]_0,z)+\omega([y,z]_0,x)+\omega([z,x]_0,y)=0, \qquad x,y,z \in \mathfrak{L} .
\end{equation}
The \emph{central extension} $\widehat{\mathfrak{L}}=\mathfrak{L} \oplus Z$ is the Lie algebra with bracket
$$[x+u,\;y+v]=[x,y]_0+\omega(x,y), \qquad x,y \in \mathfrak{L},\ u,v \in Z;$$
thus $Z$ is contained in the centre of $\widehat{\mathfrak{L}}$ and the projection
$\pi \colon \widehat{\mathfrak{L}}\to \mathfrak{L}$ along $Z$ is a homomorphism of Lie algebras.
<!-- end definition-16 -->
<!-- lemma-5: body_md -->
\label{lem:cproj}
Let $\varphi$ be a $\mathrm{Hom}$-Lie structure of $\widehat{\mathfrak{L}}$.  Then
$\overline{\varphi}:=\pi \circ \varphi|_{\mathfrak{L}}$ is a $\mathrm{Hom}$-Lie structure of $\mathfrak{L}$.
<!-- end lemma-5 -->
<!-- lemma-6: body_md -->
\label{lem:clift}
Every $\varphi \in \mathrm{End}(\widehat{\mathfrak{L}})$ can be written uniquely as
$$\varphi(x+u)=\psi(x)+f(x+u)+w(u) \qquad (x \in \mathfrak{L},\ u \in Z)$$
with $\psi \in \mathrm{End}(\mathfrak{L})$, $f \colon \widehat{\mathfrak{L}}\to Z$ linear and
$w \colon Z \to \mathfrak{L}$ linear.  Such a $\varphi$ is a $\mathrm{Hom}$-Lie structure of $\widehat{\mathfrak{L}}$ if
and only if
\begin{enumerate}
\item $\psi$ is a $\mathrm{Hom}$-Lie structure of $\mathfrak{L}$;
\item $\Omega_{\psi}=0$;
\item $[w(u),[y,z]]=0$ for all $u \in Z$ and all $y,z \in \widehat{\mathfrak{L}}$.
\end{enumerate}
In particular the ``central part'' $f$ is arbitrary, and if $w=0$ --- that is, if $\varphi(Z)
\subseteq Z$ --- then condition (3) is automatic.
<!-- end lemma-6 -->
<!-- corollary-11: body_md -->
\label{cor:cext0}
Let $\psi \in \mathrm{End}(\mathfrak{L})$ and let $\mathrm{rad}(\omega)=\{x \in \mathfrak{L} : \omega(x,\mathfrak{L})=0\}$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item If $\psi(\mathfrak{L})\subseteq \mathrm{rad}(\omega)$, then $\Omega_{\psi}=0$.
\item $\Omega_{\alpha\,\mathrm{id}}=0$ for every scalar $\alpha$.
\item If $\omega$ is a coboundary, i.e. $\omega(x,y)=g([x,y]_0)$ for some linear
$g \colon \mathfrak{L} \to Z$, then $\Omega_{\psi}=0$ for every $\mathrm{Hom}$-Lie structure $\psi$ of $\mathfrak{L}$.
Consequently $\Omega_{\psi}$ only depends on the cohomology class of $\omega$, as long as $\psi$
is a $\mathrm{Hom}$-Lie structure of $\mathfrak{L}$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end corollary-11 -->
<!-- lemma-7: body_md -->
\label{lem:cpull}
Let $p \colon \mathfrak{L} \to A$ be a surjective homomorphism of Lie algebras, let $\omega_A$ be a
$Z$-valued $2$-cocycle on $A$ and let $\omega=p^{*}\omega_A$, i.e.
$\omega(x,y)=\omega_A(p(x),p(y))$; then $\omega$ is a $2$-cocycle on $\mathfrak{L}$.  If
$\psi \in \mathrm{End}(\mathfrak{L})$ and $\psi_A \in \mathrm{End}(A)$ satisfy $p \circ \psi = \psi_A \circ p$, then
$$\Omega^{\omega}_{\psi}(x,y,z)=\Omega^{\omega_A}_{\psi_A}\big(p(x),p(y),p(z)\big),
\qquad x,y,z \in \mathfrak{L} .$$
In particular $\Omega^{\omega}_{\psi}=0$ whenever $\psi(\mathfrak{L})\subseteq \ker p$.
<!-- end lemma-7 -->
<!-- lemma-8: body_md -->
\label{lem:cubic}
Let $\mathbb{F}$ be a field of characteristic zero.
\begin{enumerate}
\item For all $A,B,C \in \mathbb{F}$,
$$(C-B)f(A)+(A-C)f(B)+(B-A)f(C)=(A-B)(B-C)(C-A)(A+B+C).$$
\item For all $u,v,w \in \mathbb{F}$,
$$(w-v)g(u)+(u-w)g(v)+(v-u)g(w)=(u-v)(v-w)(w-u)(u+v+w-3).$$
\item If $\Gamma$ is a non-trivial additive subgroup of $\mathbb{F}$ and $s \in \Gamma$, there are
$\alpha,\beta,\gamma \in \Gamma$ with $\alpha+\beta+\gamma=s$ and
$(\alpha-\beta)(\beta-\gamma)(\gamma-\alpha)\neq 0$.  The same holds for $\Gamma=\mathbb{Z}$ and
$s \in \mathbb{Z}$.
\item For all $m,n \in \mathbb{F}$,
$$(n-m)f(m+n)+(m+2n)f(m)-(2m+n)f(n)=0 .$$
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end lemma-8 -->
<!-- definition-17: body_md -->
\label{def:dghv}
Let $G$ be a non-trivial additive subgroup of $\mathbb{F}$ and let $\lambda \in \mathbb{F}$.  The
\emph{centreless deformed generalized Heisenberg--Virasoro algebra} $\check{g}(G,\lambda)$ has
basis $\{L_a,I_a\}_{a \in G}$ and multiplication
$$[L_a,L_b]=(b-a)L_{a+b}, \qquad [L_a,I_b]=(b-\lambda a)I_{a+b}, \qquad [I_a,I_b]=0 .$$
The \emph{deformed generalized Heisenberg--Virasoro algebra} $g(G,\lambda)$ is the central
extension $\check{g}(G,\lambda)\oplus Z$ of Definition \ref{def:cext} given by the cocycle
\begin{align*}
\omega(L_a,L_b)&=\delta_{a+b,0}\,\tfrac{a^3-a}{12}\,C_L, &
\omega(L_a,I_b)&=\delta_{a+b,0}\,h(a)\,C_{LI}, &
\omega(I_a,I_b)&=\delta_{a+b,0}\,a\,\delta_{\lambda,0}\,C_I,
\end{align*}
where
$$h(a)=\begin{cases}
a^2+a, & \lambda=0,\\
\frac{a^3-a}{12}, & \lambda=1,\\
\ell(a), & \lambda=-2,\\
0, & \text{otherwise},
\end{cases}$$
and, in the case $\lambda=-2$, $G$ is free of rank $\nu$ with a fixed $\mathbb{Z}$-basis
$\varepsilon_1,\dots,\varepsilon_{\nu}$ and $\ell$ is one of the coordinate forms
$a \mapsto a_{(i)}$, $2 \leq i \leq \nu$ (for $\nu \geq 2$ there are $\nu-1$ independent central
elements $C^{(i)}_{LI}$; all the statements below are to be read for each of them separately).
The centre $Z$ is spanned by the central elements which actually occur.  For $G=\mathbb{Z}$ and
$\lambda=0$ the algebra $g(\mathbb{Z},0)$ is the twisted Heisenberg--Virasoro algebra.
<!-- end definition-17 -->
<!-- definition-18: body_md -->
\label{def:dghvshift}
For $t \in G$, $\alpha,\beta,\gamma \in \mathbb{F}$, a linear map $f \colon g(G,\lambda)\to Z$ and
elements $z_s \in Z$, let $\varphi$ be the linear map of $g(G,\lambda)$ given by
$$\varphi(L_a)=\alpha L_{a+t}+\beta I_{a+t}+f(L_a), \qquad
\varphi(I_a)=\gamma I_{a+t}+f(I_a), \qquad \varphi(C_s)=z_s$$
for the central generators $C_s$ of $Z$.  We call such a map a \emph{graded shift of degree $t$
of $g(G,\lambda)$}.
<!-- end definition-18 -->
<!-- lemma-9: body_md -->
\label{lem:thvobstr}
Let $A$ be the Lie algebra with basis $\{L_a,I_a\}_{a \in G}$ and
$[L_a,L_b]=(b-a)L_{a+b}$, $[L_a,I_b]=bI_{a+b}$, $[I_a,I_b]=0$ (that is,
$A=\check{g}(G,0)$), and let $\omega_A$ be the cocycle
$$\omega_A(L_a,L_b)=\delta_{a+b,0}\tfrac{a^3-a}{12}C_L, \quad
\omega_A(L_a,I_b)=\delta_{a+b,0}h(a)C_{LI}, \quad
\omega_A(I_a,I_b)=\delta_{a+b,0}\,a\,C_I$$
with $h(a)=a^2+\kappa a$ for some $\kappa \in \mathbb{F}$.  Let
$\psi(L_a)=\alpha L_{a+t}+\beta I_{a+t}$ and $\psi(I_a)=\gamma I_{a+t}$ with $\gamma=\alpha$.
Then $\Omega_{\psi}=0$ if and only if $\beta=0$ and $\alpha t=0$.
<!-- end lemma-9 -->
<!-- theorem-17: body_md -->
\label{thm:dghv}
Let $\varphi$ be a graded shift of degree $t$ of $g(G,\lambda)$ as in Definition
\ref{def:dghvshift}.  Then $\varphi$ is a $\mathrm{Hom}$-Lie structure of $g(G,\lambda)$ if and only if
$$\gamma=\alpha, \qquad \alpha\,t=0,$$
together with
$$\beta\,t=0 \quad \text{if } \lambda=1, \qquad\qquad
\beta=0 \quad \text{if } \lambda=0, \text{ or if } \lambda=-2 \text{ and } \nu \geq 2 .$$
For all the remaining values of $\lambda$ the coefficient $\beta$ is arbitrary.
<!-- end theorem-17 -->
<!-- corollary-12: body_md -->
\label{cor:dghv}
Let $t \in G$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item If $\lambda \notin \{0,1,-2\}$, then $\psi_{t,\beta}\colon L_a \mapsto \beta I_{a+t}$,
$I_a \mapsto 0$, $C_s \mapsto 0$ is a $\mathrm{Hom}$-Lie structure of $g(G,\lambda)$ for every
$\beta \in \mathbb{F}$; consequently $\mathcal{H}(g(G,\lambda))$ contains an infinite-dimensional space
of $\mathrm{Hom}$-Lie structures which are pairwise non-congruent modulo the maps with central image.
\item If $\lambda=0$, or if $\lambda=-2$ and $\nu \geq 2$, then every graded shift which is a
$\mathrm{Hom}$-Lie structure of $g(G,\lambda)$ is of the form $\alpha\,\mathrm{id}+(\text{a map into }Z)$ on
$\check{g}(G,\lambda)$.  In particular this holds for the twisted Heisenberg--Virasoro algebra
$g(\mathbb{Z},0)$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end corollary-12 -->
<!-- remark-25: body_md -->
\label{rem:dghv}
By \cite{KKhS24b} the algebras $g(G,\lambda)$ have non-trivial $\frac12$-derivations, and hence
non-trivial transposed Poisson structures, only for $\lambda=-1$.  Theorem \ref{thm:dghv} shows
that the $\mathrm{Hom}$-Lie picture is again different, but in a weaker way than for the centreless
algebras of Section \ref{sec:wab}: the vertical shifts $\psi_{t,\beta}$ survive for all
$\lambda \notin \{0,1,-2\}$, while for $\lambda \in \{0,-2\}$ --- in particular for the twisted
Heisenberg--Virasoro algebra --- the central terms $C_I$ and $C^{(i)}_{LI}$ destroy even those,
and only the trivial graded shifts remain.  Compare Theorem \ref{thm:hv} and Corollary
\ref{cor:wabpsi}, where $\psi_{t,\beta}$ was a $\mathrm{Hom}$-Lie structure for \emph{all} $a$ and $b$.
<!-- end remark-25 -->
<!-- definition-19: body_md -->
\label{def:hatw}
The \emph{not-finitely graded Heisenberg--Virasoro algebra} $\widehat{W}(G)$ is the central
extension $W(G)_{+}\oplus \mathbb{F} C$ given by the cocycle
$$\omega(L_{\alpha,i},L_{\beta,j})
=\delta_{\alpha+\beta,0}\,\delta_{i,0}\,\delta_{j,0}\,\tfrac{\alpha^3-\alpha}{12}\,C .$$
<!-- end definition-19 -->
<!-- theorem-18: body_md -->
\label{thm:hatw}
Let $d \in G$, $m \in \mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}$, $c \in \mathbb{F}$, let $f \colon \widehat{W}(G)\to \mathbb{F} C$ be a
linear map and $z \in \mathbb{F} C$, and let $\varphi$ be the graded shift
$$\varphi(L_{\alpha,i})=c\,L_{\alpha+d,i+m}+f(L_{\alpha,i}), \qquad \varphi(C)=z .$$
Then $\varphi$ is a $\mathrm{Hom}$-Lie structure of $\widehat{W}(G)$ if and only if
$$m \geq 1 \qquad \text{or} \qquad c\,d=0 .$$
<!-- end theorem-18 -->
<!-- remark-26: body_md -->
\label{rem:hatwdelta}
By \cite{KKhS24b}, $\Delta(\widehat{W}(G))=\langle \mathrm{id},\varphi\rangle$, where $\varphi$ runs
through the maps $L_{\alpha,i}\mapsto \sum_{d \in G}\sum_{k \geq 1}a^{d,k}L_{\alpha+d,i+k}$.
These are exactly the linear combinations of the graded shifts allowed by Theorem
\ref{thm:hatw}: here the graded part of $\mathcal{H}$ and $\Delta$ coincide, in sharp contrast
with the centreless algebras of Sections \ref{sec:wab}--\ref{sec:nfg}.  The reason is
structural: the shifts with $m \geq 1$ survive because they take values in the ideal
$\mathcal{I}_{+}$, on which the cocycle vanishes.
<!-- end remark-26 -->
<!-- definition-20: body_md -->
\label{def:tildew}
The algebra $\widetilde{W}(G)$ is the central extension $W_{-1}(G)\oplus \mathbb{F} C$ (Definition
\ref{def:wng} with $n=-1$, the second index running over $\mathbb{Z}$) given by the cocycle
$$\omega(L_{\alpha,i},L_{\beta,j})=\delta_{\alpha+\beta,0}\Big(\delta_{i+j,-1}\alpha^3
+3i\,\delta_{i+j,0}\alpha^2+3i(i-1)\delta_{i+j,1}\alpha+i(i-1)(i-2)\delta_{i+j,2}\Big)C .$$
<!-- end definition-20 -->
<!-- theorem-19: body_md -->
\label{thm:tildew}
Let $d \in G$, $m \in \mathbb{Z}$, $c \in \mathbb{F}$, let $f \colon \widetilde{W}(G)\to \mathbb{F} C$ be linear and
$z \in \mathbb{F} C$, and let $\varphi$ be the graded shift
$$\varphi(L_{\alpha,i})=c\,L_{\alpha+d,i+m}+f(L_{\alpha,i}), \qquad \varphi(C)=z .$$
Then $\varphi$ is a $\mathrm{Hom}$-Lie structure of $\widetilde{W}(G)$ if and only if
$$c\,d=0 \qquad \text{and} \qquad c\,m=0,$$
that is, if and only if $\varphi$ is a scalar multiple of the identity modulo the centre.
<!-- end theorem-19 -->
<!-- remark-27: body_md -->
\label{rem:tildewdelta}
By \cite{KKhS24b}, $\Delta(\widetilde{W}(G))=\langle \mathrm{id} \rangle$ and $\widetilde{W}(G)$ has no
non-trivial transposed Poisson structure.  Theorem \ref{thm:tildew} shows that, for graded
shifts, the $\mathrm{Hom}$-Lie structures behave in the same way.  The contrast with Theorem
\ref{thm:hatw} is instructive: for $\widehat{W}(G)$ the cocycle is concentrated on the level
$i=0$, which is a quotient of the algebra, whereas the cocycle of $\widetilde{W}(G)$ involves
four levels, and the shifts in the $i$-direction can no longer avoid it.
<!-- end remark-27 -->
<!-- proposition-4: body_md -->
\label{prop:hwjac}
The multiplication (\ref{hwt1})--(\ref{hwt3}) does not satisfy the Jacobi identity.  Explicitly,
$$\big[L_{-3,0},[L_{0,0},L_{3,1}]\big]+\big[L_{0,0},[L_{3,1},L_{-3,0}]\big]
+\big[L_{3,1},[L_{-3,0},L_{0,0}]\big]=-2\,C_L \neq 0 .$$
<!-- end proposition-4 -->
<!-- definition-21: body_md -->
\label{def:hwhat}
Let $\widetilde{HW}_1(G)=HW(G)_{+}\oplus \langle C_L,C_{LH},C_H\rangle$ be the central extension
of $HW(G)_{+}\subseteq HW_1(G)$ given by the cocycle
\begin{align*}
\omega(L_{\alpha,i},L_{\beta,j})&=\delta_{\alpha+\beta,0}\delta_{i,0}\delta_{j,0}
\tfrac{\alpha^3-\alpha}{12}C_L, &
\omega(L_{\alpha,i},H_{\beta,j})&=\delta_{\alpha+\beta,0}\delta_{i,0}\delta_{j,0}
(\alpha^2-\alpha)C_{LH}, \\
\omega(H_{\alpha,i},H_{\beta,j})&=\delta_{\alpha+\beta,0}\delta_{i,0}\delta_{j,0}\,\alpha\,C_H. &&
\end{align*}
<!-- end definition-21 -->
<!-- proposition-5: body_md -->
\label{prop:hwhatlie}
$\widetilde{HW}_1(G)$ is a Lie algebra, i.e. the above $\omega$ satisfies (\ref{cocycle}).
<!-- end proposition-5 -->
<!-- theorem-20: body_md -->
\label{thm:hwhat}
Let $d \in G$, $m \in \mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}$, $a,b,g \in \mathbb{F}$, let $f$ be a linear map of
$\widetilde{HW}_1(G)$ into its centre $Z=\langle C_L,C_{LH},C_H\rangle$ and let
$z_L,z_{LH},z_H \in Z$.  Let $\varphi$ be the graded shift
$$\varphi(L_{\alpha,i})=a\,L_{\alpha+d,i+m}+b\,H_{\alpha+d,i+m}+f(L_{\alpha,i}), \qquad
\varphi(H_{\alpha,i})=g\,H_{\alpha+d,i+m}+f(H_{\alpha,i}),$$
$\varphi(C_L)=z_L$, $\varphi(C_{LH})=z_{LH}$, $\varphi(C_H)=z_H$.  Then $\varphi$ is a
$\mathrm{Hom}$-Lie structure of $\widetilde{HW}_1(G)$ if and only if
$$a=g, \qquad a\,d=0, \qquad a\,m=0, \qquad \text{and} \qquad b=0 \ \text{ if } m=0 .$$
<!-- end theorem-20 -->
<!-- remark-28: body_md -->
\label{rem:hwhat}
Thus $\widetilde{HW}_1(G)$ behaves like $\widehat{W}(G)$ in the $i$-direction and like the
twisted Heisenberg--Virasoro algebra in the $\alpha$-direction: the only graded shifts which are
$\mathrm{Hom}$-Lie structures and are non-trivial modulo the centre are the maps
$L_{\alpha,i}\mapsto b\,H_{\alpha+d,i+m}$, $H_{\alpha,i}\mapsto 0$ with $m \geq 1$, which take
their values in the ideal $\mathcal{J}_{+}$ on which the cocycle vanishes.  In particular
$\mathcal{H}(\widetilde{HW}_1(G))$ is infinite-dimensional modulo the maps with central image.
<!-- end remark-28 -->
<!-- definition-22: body_md -->
\label{def:esv}
The \emph{extended Schr\"odinger--Virasoro algebra} $\hat{\mathfrak{so}}$ is the central
extension of the extended Schr\"odinger--Witt algebra $\widetilde{\mathfrak{so}}$ of Definition
\ref{def:eschro} by $Z=\langle C_L,C_{LN},C_N\rangle$ given by the cocycle
$$\omega(L_m,L_n)=\delta_{m+n,0}\tfrac{m^3-m}{12}C_L, \quad
\omega(L_m,N_n)=\delta_{m+n,0}(m^2-m)C_{LN}, \quad
\omega(N_m,N_n)=\delta_{m+n,0}\,n\,C_N,$$
all the other values of $\omega$ on pairs of basis vectors being zero.
<!-- end definition-22 -->
<!-- theorem-21: body_md -->
\label{thm:esv}
For every $t \in \mathbb{Z}$ and every $\beta \in \mathbb{F}$ let $\hat\chi_{t,\beta}$ be the linear map of
$\hat{\mathfrak{so}}$ with
$$\hat\chi_{t,\beta}(L_m)=\beta M_{m+t}, \qquad
\hat\chi_{t,\beta}(M_n)=\hat\chi_{t,\beta}(N_n)=\hat\chi_{t,\beta}(Y_{n+\frac12})=0, \qquad
\hat\chi_{t,\beta}(Z)=0 .$$
Then $\hat\chi_{t,\beta}$ is a $\mathrm{Hom}$-Lie structure of $\hat{\mathfrak{so}}$, and so is every map
$$\varphi=\alpha\,\mathrm{id}+\sum_{t \in S}\hat\chi_{t,\beta_t}+f(\cdot), \qquad
S \subseteq \mathbb{Z} \ \text{finite},$$
where $\alpha,\beta_t \in \mathbb{F}$ and $f$ is an arbitrary linear map of $\hat{\mathfrak{so}}$ into
its centre.  In particular $\mathcal{H}(\hat{\mathfrak{so}})$ contains an infinite-dimensional
space of $\mathrm{Hom}$-Lie structures which are pairwise non-congruent modulo the maps with central
image.
<!-- end theorem-21 -->
<!-- remark-29: body_md -->
\label{rem:esv}
By \cite{Sh24} the algebra $\hat{\mathfrak{so}}$ has no non-trivial $\frac12$-derivation, and
hence no non-trivial transposed Poisson structure.  Together with Theorem \ref{thm:eschro} and
Remark \ref{rem:eschro} this gives a second, and even more rigid, example of the phenomenon of
Remark \ref{rem:halfstrict}: for both $\widetilde{\mathfrak{so}}$ and its central extension
$\hat{\mathfrak{so}}$ the space of $\frac12$-derivations is $\langle \mathrm{id}\rangle$, while the space
of $\mathrm{Hom}$-Lie structures is infinite-dimensional even modulo the centre.  In contrast with the
Virasoro algebra (Remark \ref{rem:vir}) and with the twisted Heisenberg--Virasoro algebra
(Corollary \ref{cor:dghv}(2)), passing to the central extension changes nothing here, because
the three cocycles of Definition \ref{def:esv} do not involve the abelian ideal $\mathcal{M}$ in
which the maps $\chi_{t,\beta}$ take their values.
<!-- end remark-29 -->
<!-- definition-23: body_md -->
\label{def:dsv}
The algebras $\widetilde{L_{\lambda,\mu}}^{\,i}$ are the central extensions of $L_{\lambda,\mu}$
determined by the following cocycles, where $f(x)=x^3-x$:
\begin{enumerate}
\item[$(1)$] $\omega(L_m,L_n)=\delta_{m+n,0}\frac{f(m)}{12}C_L$ \quad
($\mu \notin \frac12 \mathbb{Z}$; or $\mu \in \frac12+\mathbb{Z}$ and $\lambda \neq -3,-1,1$; or
$\mu \in \mathbb{Z}$ and $\lambda \neq -1$);
\item[$(2)$] the cocycle of $(1)$ together with
$\omega(L_m,Y_{n+\frac12})=\delta_{m+n+\mu+\frac12,0}C_{LY}$ \quad
($\mu \in \frac12+\mathbb{Z}$, $\lambda=-3$);
\item[$(3)$] the cocycle of $(1)$ together with
$\omega(L_m,Y_{n+\frac12})=\frac{m(m-1)}{2}\delta_{m+n+\mu+\frac12,0}C_{LY}$ and
$\omega(M_m,Y_{n+\frac12})=\delta_{m+n+3\mu+\frac12,0}C_{MY}$ \quad
($\mu \in \frac12+\mathbb{Z}$, $\lambda=-1$);
\item[$(5)$] the cocycle of $(1)$ together with
$\omega(Y_{m+\frac12},Y_{n+\frac12})=-(m+\mu+\frac12)\delta_{m+n+2\mu+1,0}C_Y$ \quad
($\mu \in \mathbb{Z}$, $\lambda=-1$).
\end{enumerate}
The remaining case $\widetilde{L_{1,\mu}}^{\,4}$ ($\mu \in \frac12+\mathbb{Z}$, $\lambda=1$) is
discussed in Proposition \ref{prop:l4jac} and Definition \ref{def:l4} below.
<!-- end definition-23 -->
<!-- definition-24: body_md -->
\label{def:dsvshift}
For $t \in \mathbb{Z}$, $\alpha,\beta,\gamma,\delta \in \mathbb{F}$, a linear map $f$ of
$\widetilde{L_{\lambda,\mu}}^{\,i}$ into its centre $Z$ and elements $z_s \in Z$, the
\emph{graded shift of degree $t$} is the linear map $\varphi$ with
$$\varphi(L_m)=\alpha L_{m+t}+\beta M_{m+t}+f(L_m), \qquad
\varphi(M_m)=\gamma M_{m+t}+f(M_m),$$
$$\varphi(Y_{m+\frac12})=\delta Y_{m+t+\frac12}+f(Y_{m+\frac12}), \qquad \varphi(C_s)=z_s .$$
<!-- end definition-24 -->
<!-- theorem-22: body_md -->
\label{thm:dsv}
Let $i \in \{1,2,3,5\}$ and let $\varphi$ be a graded shift of degree $t$ of
$\widetilde{L_{\lambda,\mu}}^{\,i}$.  Then $\varphi$ is a $\mathrm{Hom}$-Lie structure if and only if
$$\gamma=\delta=\alpha \qquad \text{and} \qquad \alpha\,t=0 .$$
In particular the coefficient $\beta$ is arbitrary, so that
$\mathcal{H}(\widetilde{L_{\lambda,\mu}}^{\,i})$ is infinite-dimensional modulo the maps with
central image.
<!-- end theorem-22 -->
<!-- remark-30: body_md -->
\label{rem:dsvhalf}
By \cite{Sh24}, $\widetilde{L_{\lambda,\mu}}^{\,i}$ has no non-trivial $\frac12$-derivation for
$i \in \{2,3,5\}$ and for $i=1$ with $\lambda \neq 1$, while
$\Delta(\widetilde{L_{1,\mu}}^{\,1})$ consists of the maps
$$L_m \mapsto \lambda_1 L_m+\sum_t \alpha_t M_{m+t}+\sum_t \beta_t Y_{m+t+\frac12}, \quad
Y_{m+\frac12}\mapsto \lambda_1Y_{m+\frac12}+\sum_t\beta_tM_{m+t+1}, \quad
M_m \mapsto \lambda_1 M_m .$$
The maps with $\beta_t \neq 0$ are homogeneous of half-integer degree and are therefore not
graded shifts in the sense of Definition \ref{def:dsvshift}; by Theorem \ref{thm:half} they are
$\mathrm{Hom}$-Lie structures as well.  The maps with $\alpha_t \neq 0$ are linear combinations of the
graded shifts $\psi_{0,t}\colon L_m\mapsto M_{m+t}$, $M\mapsto 0$, $Y\mapsto 0$ (Definition
\ref{def:dsvshift} with $\alpha=\gamma=\delta=0$, $\beta=1$ and $f=0$), which Theorem
\ref{thm:dsv} exhibits as $\mathrm{Hom}$-Lie structures for \emph{all} $\lambda$ and $\mu$.
<!-- end remark-30 -->
<!-- proposition-6: body_md -->
\label{prop:l4jac}
The multiplication (\ref{l4a})--(\ref{l4d}) does not satisfy the Jacobi identity.  For
$\mu=\frac12$,
$$\big[L_0,[Y_{\frac12},Y_{-\frac12}]\big]+\big[Y_{\frac12},[Y_{-\frac12},L_0]\big]
+\big[Y_{-\frac12},[L_0,Y_{\frac12}]\big]=-\tfrac38\,C_M \neq 0 .$$
More precisely, the two central terms of (\ref{l4c}) and (\ref{l4d}) are supported on pairs of
different total degree: with $\deg L_m=m$, $\deg M_n=n$ and $\deg Y_{n+\frac12}=n+\frac12$, the
first is supported in degree $-2\mu$ and the second in degree $-2\mu+1$.  For such a pair of
supports the cocycle identity (\ref{cocycle}) for the triples $(L,Y,Y)$ forces the central term
of (\ref{l4c}) to vanish identically.
<!-- end proposition-6 -->
<!-- definition-25: body_md -->
\label{def:l4}
Let $\mu \in \frac12+\mathbb{Z}$.  The algebra $\widetilde{L_{1,\mu}}^{\,4}$ is the central extension of
$L_{1,\mu}$ by $Z=\langle C_L,C_{LY},C_M\rangle$ given by the cocycle
\begin{align*}
\omega(L_m,L_n)&=\delta_{m+n,0}\tfrac{f(m)}{12}C_L, &
\omega(L_m,Y_{n+\frac12})&=-f(m)\,\delta_{m+n+\mu+\frac12,0}C_{LY},\\
\omega(L_m,M_n)&=-f(m)\,\delta_{m+n+2\mu,0}C_M, &
\omega(Y_{m+\frac12},Y_{n+\frac12})&=-f\big(m+\mu+\tfrac12\big)\,
\delta_{m+n+2\mu+1,0}C_M,
\end{align*}
where $f(x)=x^3-x$.  This is (\ref{l4a})--(\ref{l4d}) with the last line corrected; the
coefficient $-m(m^2-1)=-f(m)$ of (\ref{l4b}) and (\ref{l4c}) is unchanged.
<!-- end definition-25 -->
<!-- proposition-7: body_md -->
\label{prop:l4lie}
The cocycle of Definition \ref{def:l4} satisfies (\ref{cocycle}), so that
$\widetilde{L_{1,\mu}}^{\,4}$ is a Lie algebra.
<!-- end proposition-7 -->
<!-- theorem-23: body_md -->
\label{thm:l4}
Let $\mu \in \frac12+\mathbb{Z}$ and let $\varphi$ be a graded shift of degree $t$ of
$\widetilde{L_{1,\mu}}^{\,4}$ as in Definition \ref{def:dsvshift}.  Then $\varphi$ is a
$\mathrm{Hom}$-Lie structure if and only if
$$\gamma=\delta=\alpha, \qquad \alpha\,t=0, \qquad \beta\,(t+2\mu)=0 .$$
<!-- end theorem-23 -->
<!-- remark-31: body_md -->
\label{rem:l4}
Theorem \ref{thm:l4} is the only place in this paper where a non-trivial graded shift of
non-zero degree survives in a central extension for one single value of the degree: the map
$L_m \mapsto \beta M_{m-2\mu}$, $M \mapsto 0$, $Y \mapsto 0$ is a $\mathrm{Hom}$-Lie structure of
$\widetilde{L_{1,\mu}}^{\,4}$, and no other map $\psi_{0,t}\colon L_m\mapsto M_{m+t}$,
$M\mapsto 0$, $Y\mapsto 0$ is.  The reason is that the cocycle of Definition \ref{def:l4} pairs
